Your model overfits the training data. It learned specific patterns and noise from the training set. These patterns do not occur in new data. For this reason, performance on new data is much lower.

This pattern usually indicates overfitting. It can also indicate data leakage or a distribution shift.

Steps

1. Split your data into a training set, a validation set, and a test set.
2. Use the test set only at the end.
3. Check for data leakage between the training and test sets.
4. Check that the new data comes from the same distribution as the training data.
5. If the distribution differs, collect data from the target distribution.
6. If you can, get more training data.
7. Reduce the model complexity.
8. Add L1 or L2 regularization to the loss function.
9. Stop training when the validation loss increases for several epochs.
10. Use data augmentation on the training examples.
11. Remove irrelevant features.
12. Use cross-validation to check that the model performs well on different data splits.
13. Average the predictions from several models with different initializations.

Smoke alarm types, placement, and care

General notes
The label "general guidance" identifies common practice and recommendations. These statements are not universal requirements. The alarm instructions, laws, and local fire or building codes contain requirements. You must follow them. The word "must" marks a requirement from those sources. Other statements are general guidance.

Types of smoke alarms
Ionization alarms respond faster to fires that produce small smoke particles. They use a small radioactive source to ionize air in a detection chamber. Smoke particles attach to ions. That action reduces the electric current. The alarm sounds when the current drops below a set level.
Photoelectric alarms respond faster to fires that produce larger smoke particles. They use a light beam and a light sensor in a chamber. Smoke particles scatter the light. The alarm sounds when the sensor receives the scattered light.
Dual-sensor alarms contain both methods in one unit. They detect both fire types. Their performance depends on the design and the alarm standard.
No alarm type is best for all fires. Many fire safety organizations recommend photoelectric alarms or dual-sensor alarms. That recommendation is not a universal legal requirement.

Placement
General guidance:
Install alarms on every level of the home.
Install alarms inside each bedroom.
Install alarms outside each separate bedroom.
Put alarms on the ceiling or high on a wall.
Keep alarms away from kitchens, bathrooms, and vents.
Requirement check:
Check your local code for exact required locations.
Check the alarm instructions for distance limits from walls, corners, kitchens, bathrooms, and vents.
Follow those limits.

Interconnection
General guidance:
Interconnected alarms sound together. When one alarm detects smoke, all connected alarms sound.
Wired interconnection uses a signal wire between alarms. Wireless interconnection uses radio signals.
Some alarms connect to home power with a battery backup. Other alarms use only batteries.
Interconnection helps people in other rooms hear the alarm.
Requirement check:
Check your local code for interconnection requirements.
Use compatible alarms. Use alarms of the same brand and model family if the instructions require that.
Check the alarm instructions before you add or replace an alarm.

Routine care

Test the alarms
1. Read the alarm instructions before you start.
2. Test each alarm at least once each month.
3. Press the test button until the alarm sounds.
4. If the alarm does not sound, check the battery and replace it if needed.
5. If the alarm still does not sound, replace the alarm.
Do not test with flame or smoke. Some instructions permit a listed test product. Use only the test method in the instructions.
Note: On many alarms, the test button checks power and sounder only. It does not check sensor response to smoke. The instructions state what the test covers.

Clean the alarms
1. Clean each alarm at least once each year. Some instructions require more frequent dust removal.
2. If the alarm is hardwired, switch off the circuit breaker first.
3. Remove the battery if the design permits that.
4. Use a vacuum cleaner with a soft brush attachment.
5. Remove dust from the cover and vents.
6. Do not use water, liquid cleaner, or paint on the alarm.
7. Put the battery back and switch on the circuit breaker.
8. Test the alarm after you clean it.
If the vents stay blocked, replace the alarm.

Replace batteries
1. Check the battery type and replacement steps in the instructions.
2. Replace a removable battery at least once each year.
3. Replace the battery immediately when the low-battery signal sounds.
4. Some alarms have sealed batteries. You cannot replace those batteries. For those alarms, replace the whole alarm when the end-of-life signal sounds.
5. After you install a new battery, press the test button.
6. If the alarm still chirps, check the battery orientation. Install it again if needed.
7. If the chirp continues, replace the alarm.
Many people replace batteries when clocks change for daylight time. That is a reminder only, not a code requirement.

Replace old alarms
1. Find the manufacture date on the alarm label.
2. If the manufacture date is missing or unreadable, replace the alarm.
3. Many alarms have a service life of 10 years from the manufacture date. Some alarms have a different service life. Replace the alarm when it reaches the end of its service life.
4. Replace an alarm if it fails a test after battery replacement.
5. Replace an alarm if it is painted, damaged, or exposed to a fire.
6. If the alarm sounds an end-of-life signal, replace the alarm.
7. Dispose of ionization alarms as local rules require. They contain a small radioactive source.
For hardwired alarm replacement:
1. Read the instructions for the new alarm.
2. Switch off the circuit breaker for the old alarm.
3. Remove the old alarm from its base.
4. Attach the new alarm to the current wiring only if the instructions permit that.
5. Insert or activate the battery as the instructions state.
6. Restore power and test the alarm.
7. Check that all interconnected alarms still work together.

Record these assumptions and limitations before you make a causal interpretation.

Assumptions
- No unmeasured confounding: all common causes of the exposure and the outcome are measured and adjusted for.
- Positivity: each unit has a non-zero probability of each exposure level within all covariate strata.
- Consistency: the observed outcome equals the potential outcome for the observed exposure.
- No interference: one unit's exposure does not affect another unit's outcome.
- Correct model specification: the functional forms, interactions, and distributions are correct.
- No measurement error: exposure, outcome, and covariates are measured without error.
- No selection bias: the analyzed sample represents the target population after adjustment.
- Temporal order is established: the exposure precedes the outcome.

Limitations
- Residual confounding can remain from unmeasured or imperfectly measured confounders.
- Measurement error can bias estimates, often toward the null or in unpredictable directions.
- Missing data can cause selection bias if the missingness relates to both exposure and outcome.
- Time-varying confounding affected by prior exposure can bias standard adjustment methods.
- Immortal time bias can arise if the exposure definition requires survival to a later time.
- Model dependence: results can change under alternative plausible model specifications.
- Multiple comparisons can produce false positive findings when many exposures or outcomes are tested.
- Generalizability is limited to populations similar to the study sample.

The causal interpretation is valid only if these assumptions hold. The assumptions are not directly verifiable from the data.

This text describes the responsibilities and delegation behavior of the JVM built-in class loaders. It also outlines trade-offs for a custom class loader. The behavior depends on the JVM implementation and version. The description applies to Java SE 9 and later. In Java 8, the names differ.

The JVM has three built-in class loaders. The bootstrap class loader loads core Java classes from the runtime image. The platform class loader loads Java SE platform classes and JDK classes. The system class loader loads application classes from the class path and the module path. The bootstrap class loader has no parent. The platform class loader's parent is the bootstrap class loader, and the system class loader's parent is the platform class loader.

Built-in loaders use parent-first delegation. A class loader asks its parent to load a class before it tries to load the class itself. The parent asks its own parent, up to the bootstrap class loader. If a parent cannot load the class, the child tries. This process prevents duplicate copies of core classes. It preserves type identity across the JVM.

A custom class loader can change this delegation. The class loader API allows an implementation to load a class before it asks the parent. This is child-first delegation. Child-first delegation gives application isolation. It also creates a risk of duplicate class definitions, and built-in loaders cannot use child-first delegation. The runtime fixes their delegation.

A custom class loader for application isolation offers these trade-offs:
- Isolation: child-first lets each application use its own library versions.
- Duplicate classes: memory use increases because each loader keeps separate copies.
- Type identity: a class loaded by two different loaders is two distinct types. A cast between them fails at runtime.
- Complexity: the custom loader must implement a cache, concurrency control, and resource resolution.
- Security: the loader must obey Java module accessibility and package sealing rules.
- Performance and compatibility: custom delegation adds overhead, and frameworks that use the thread context class loader can fail.

The following details belong in the documentation. The invokedynamic instruction does late linkage through a bootstrap method. Each occurrence of the instruction is a separate dynamic call site.

Resolution

The constant pool entry at the instruction index is a CONSTANT_InvokeDynamic. This entry holds an index into the BootstrapMethods attribute and a CONSTANT_NameAndType. The BootstrapMethods attribute entry contains a CONSTANT_MethodHandle and static arguments. The CONSTANT_NameAndType gives the call site name and the descriptor.

The JVM invokes the bootstrap method with a MethodHandles.Lookup object, the call site name, a MethodType object, and the static arguments. The Lookup object has the access privileges of the class that contains the instruction. The bootstrap method must accept the Lookup object, a String name, a MethodType, and the static argument types. The bootstrap method must return a CallSite object. The JVM links the instruction to the target handle of that call site.

Result checks

The static arguments must be loadable constants such as String, Class, Integer, Long, Float, Double, MethodHandle, or MethodType. The returned CallSite must not be null. The type of the target handle must exactly match the instruction descriptor. If the bootstrap method completes abruptly with an exception that is not an Error instance, the JVM wraps that exception in a BootstrapMethodError. If the return check or the target type check fails, the JVM throws a BootstrapMethodError.

Operand stack and local variables

The invokedynamic instruction itself does not read or write local variables. Local variable manipulation requires separate load and store instructions before and after the invokedynamic. The instruction consumes argument values from the operand stack, in descriptor order. Long and double values occupy two stack slots each. After the target executes, the instruction pushes the return value, unless the descriptor return type is void.

Edge cases

- Resolution happens lazily when the instruction first executes. If resolution fails, subsequent executions of the same instruction must throw the same BootstrapMethodError.
- If multiple threads execute the same instruction for the first time concurrently, one thread performs resolution. The other threads wait for that resolution.
- Each occurrence of the instruction has its own call site. Multiple occurrences that reference the same constant pool entry still have separate call sites.
- The call site can be a MutableCallSite or a VolatileCallSite. Later executions read the current target from that call site.
- The operand stack remains unchanged when bootstrap resolution fails. The instruction has not consumed the argument values.
- The target handle is invoked exactly, as if by MethodHandle.invokeExact. No implicit argument or return conversions occur.
- The JVM verifier checks that the operand stack types match the descriptor before the instruction executes. A mismatch causes a VerifyError.
- The JVM passes the static arguments in the order they appear in the BootstrapMethods attribute.
- If the bootstrap method reference cannot be resolved, the JVM reports a bootstrap method resolution failure.

A bounded context is a boundary around a model in a software system. Inside this boundary, each term has one explicit meaning. Outside the boundary, the same term can have a different meaning. In domain-driven design, you divide a large business domain into bounded contexts. Each bounded context contains a model and a language that the team understands.

Bounded contexts are important because they prevent model conflicts. One business term can mean different things in different parts of a company. For example, the word Customer means one concept in a sales context and a different concept in a support context. Without boundaries, a shared model forces you to merge these meanings. This merge creates confusion and defects. Separate contexts let each team change its model independently.

You can identify bounded contexts from the domain language. Different meanings of one word point to separate contexts. Business capabilities that change at different rates also suggest boundaries. Separate data ownership or separate deployment cycles provide more evidence. A context map records these boundaries and their connections.

In an online store, the Sales context manages orders and payments, and the Support context manages service tickets and returns. In the Sales context, Customer includes the invoice address and payment method. In the Support context, Customer includes contact history and issue priority. These are two bounded contexts with separate models. They can exchange data through a defined interface, for example an event that carries a customer identifier.

For this guide, low voltage means control circuits that operate below 1000 V AC. The guide must explain the design and protection trade-offs that follow. The guide must keep descriptive text and procedural text in separate sections.

Transformer size and inrush current. A larger transformer limits voltage drop when contactors and relays energize. A larger transformer also increases the available short-circuit current. The chosen size must balance these two effects.

Short-circuit protection and nuisance trip. Time-delay or dual-element fuses let inrush current pass. Fast-acting protection interrupts faults more quickly but can trip during normal coil inrush. The selected protection must clear faults and not trip on inrush.

Grounded and ungrounded control circuits. A grounded control circuit makes faults easier to locate and reduces shock risk from leakage or static. An ungrounded control circuit continues to operate after one ground fault. A second ground fault can cause an unwanted start. The guide must explain this trade-off for the specific machine.

Overcurrent protection placement. A control transformer must have primary and secondary protection as the applicable code requires. A fuse in the grounded conductor can open and leave live voltage on parts that appear de-energized. The grounded conductor must not have a fuse.

Power source selection. A dedicated control transformer isolates the control circuit from power-circuit faults and transients. A direct tap from the power circuit can expose control devices to higher fault current. The guide must state the source and its available fault current.

The guide must include the safety precautions that follow.

Use lockout and tagout. Lock out all sources of energy that supply the panel.

Identify every power source. Include sources in other panels.

Verify zero energy. Use a meter that is rated for the voltage category and the environment.

Test the meter on a known live source before and after the zero-energy check.

If the zero-energy check fails, stop work. Repeat the isolation procedure.

Use the specified personal protective equipment and insulated tools for the measured voltage.

Remove metal jewelry and wear safety glasses.

Do not rely on a pilot light or a PLC input to prove de-energization.

Treat capacitors and long cable runs as stored-energy sources. Discharge them before work.

Allow only qualified persons to open the panel. Apply local rules and facility procedures.

The guide must include these warnings.

Low voltage does not mean safe voltage. A 120 VAC control circuit can cause a lethal shock. A 24 VAC circuit can cause burns or a fire if the source can deliver enough current.

Do not defeat interlocks or safety devices.

Read the warning label on the disconnect. The label must show the voltage and the available fault current.

Spring Security manages HTTP session security through filters and strategies. Tomcat provides the servlet container session. You must configure both layers. Session fixation protection changes the session ID after authentication. Concurrent session control limits active logins per user. Logout revocation invalidates the session and removes the cookie.

PROCEDURE

1. Set session fixation protection and session rotation.
   Use the sessionManagement DSL in HttpSecurity.
   Code:
   ```
   http.sessionManagement().sessionFixation().changeSessionId();
   ```

2. Set cookie attributes.
   In Tomcat, add the CookieProcessor element to context.xml.
   Code:
   ```
   <Context>
       <CookieProcessor sameSiteCookies="strict" />
   </Context>
   ```
   Set HttpOnly and Secure flags in Spring Boot properties.
   Code:
   ```
   server.servlet.session.cookie.http-only=true
   server.servlet.session.cookie.secure=true
   server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site=strict
   ```
   If you do not use Spring Boot, configure these attributes in web.xml or with a CookieSerializer bean.
   Use the Secure attribute only when HTTPS is active.

3. Handle concurrent sessions.
   Register SessionRegistryImpl as a bean.
   Code:
   ```
   @Bean
   public SessionRegistry sessionRegistry() {
       return new SessionRegistryImpl();
   }
   ```
   Configure maximum sessions in HttpSecurity.
   Code:
   ```
   http.sessionManagement()
       .maximumSessions(1)
       .maxSessionsPreventsLogin(true);
   ```
   If you want to reject the second login, keep maxSessionsPreventsLogin as true.
   If you want to expire the first session, set maxSessionsPreventsLogin to false.
   Do not add ConcurrentSessionFilter manually. Spring Security adds it when you configure sessionManagement.

4. Handle logout revocation.
   Configure logout in HttpSecurity.
   Code:
   ```
   http.logout()
       .invalidateHttpSession(true)
       .deleteCookies("JSESSIONID")
       .logoutSuccessUrl("/login?logout");
   ```
   If you use concurrent session control, register a custom LogoutHandler.
   Call sessionRegistry.getSessionInformation(sessionId).expireNow() in that handler.

5. Handle edge cases.
   - Prevent session IDs in URLs. In Tomcat, set disableURLRewriting="true" on the Context element.
   - Set a session timeout. In Spring Boot, set server.servlet.session.timeout=15m.
   - Verify session ID rotation. Log in, record the old session ID, authenticate, and confirm that the session ID changed.
   - Verify concurrent session policy. Log in twice from two browsers. Confirm that the policy behaves as configured.

DESCRIPTIVE NOTES

These settings apply to Spring Security 5 and later, Tomcat 8.5 and later, and Servlet 3.1. You must check your versions before you apply them.

Session fixation protection: Spring Security default is changeSessionId for Servlet 3.1 containers. Tomcat 8.5 and later support Servlet 3.1. For older containers, migrateSession is the default. You can set sessionFixation().migrateSession() for older containers.

Cookie attributes: The SameSite attribute prevents cross-site request forgery. Tomcat 9.0.19 and later support sameSiteCookies on CookieProcessor. Older Tomcat versions require a custom filter or cookie serializer.

Concurrent sessions: The SessionRegistry stores session information per principal. When maxSessionsPreventsLogin is false, the least recently used session expires. When it is true, the second authentication fails with an error message. You can customize the error message with an AuthenticationFailureHandler.

Logout revocation: The LogoutHandler must invalidate the HTTP session and remove the SecurityContext. The sessionRegistry expireNow method marks the session for removal on the next request.

The disableURLRewriting property in Tomcat works only if the application does not call response.encodeURL().

WebSockets and AJAX: After logout, close any open WebSocket connections. The server session is invalid. Client-side code must handle 401 or 403 responses and redirect to login.

In classical physics, electric and magnetic fields are vector fields. Each field has a magnitude and a direction at every point in space.

Similarities

- Each field can apply a force to an object at a distance.
- Each field stores energy in the region around its source.
- Both fields can exist together in electromagnetic waves.

Differences

- An electric field applies a force to any electric charge. The charge can be at rest or in motion.
- A magnetic field applies no force to a charge at rest.
- A magnetic field applies a force to a charge that has a velocity component across the field.
- A magnetic field applies a force or a torque to a magnet.
- The electric force on a positive charge points in the direction of the electric field.
- The magnetic force is perpendicular to the charge velocity and to the magnetic field.
- An electric field can do work on a charge.
- The magnetic force does no work on a point charge. The force is perpendicular to the displacement at every instant.
- Static electric field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges.
- Magnetic field lines have no beginning or end.
- Electric charge or a magnetic field that changes with time produces an electric field.
- Electric current or an electric field that changes with time produces a magnetic field.

Electromagnetic waves

When a magnetic field changes with time, it produces an electric field. When an electric field changes with time, it produces a magnetic field. These two effects can sustain each other. A charge that accelerates creates an electric field that changes with time. That electric field produces a magnetic field. That magnetic field changes and produces an electric field.

The result is a wave that propagates through space. In a vacuum, this wave travels at the speed of light. Far from the source, the electric field and the magnetic field are perpendicular to each other. They are also perpendicular to the direction of travel. For this reason, electromagnetic waves are transverse waves. Light, radio waves, and X-rays are examples of electromagnetic waves.

The preventive maintenance documentation must include these sections.

A. Maintenance schedule
- The maintenance schedule must list each vehicle and its service intervals.
- The schedule must use the manufacturer intervals or your data for severe conditions.
- The schedule must state the tasks for each interval. Examples are oil change, filter replacement, brake inspection, and tire rotation.
- The schedule must define who approves a deferral and what conditions permit a deferral.

B. Inspection checklists
- The documentation must include one checklist for each vehicle type. Each item must have a pass or fail result.
- The checklists must use the verb "check" for inspection steps and "replace" for parts that have failed.
- The checklists must include space for notes, the technician name, and the date.

C. Work order and repair records
- The documentation must record the date, vehicle identification number, mileage, work completed, parts used, and labor hours.
- The documentation must record the cost of parts and labor for each work order.
- The records must be searchable by vehicle identification number and by date.

D. Downtime log
- The documentation must record each unplanned downtime event. The log must include the date, vehicle identification number, duration, and cause.
- The log must classify downtime as preventive maintenance, repair, parts wait, or accident.

E. Cost and reliability summary
- The summary must calculate cost per mile per vehicle for each month or quarter.
- The summary must calculate mean time between failures for each vehicle.
- The summary must calculate schedule compliance as the percent of preventive maintenance tasks completed on time.

F. Decision rules
- The documentation must include triggers for immediate action. For example, two repeat failures of the same system within 30 days can require a review of that system.
- The documentation must include thresholds for major repair versus vehicle replacement. The thresholds must use cost per mile and downtime days per month.
- The documentation must define who reviews the summary and how often.
- The rule must state that a decrease in reliability after an interval change requires a return to the previous interval.

G. Review and update procedure
- The procedure must require a review of the documentation each quarter. The review must compare cost and reliability data with the previous period.
- The procedure must allow interval updates only if the data show a clear trend. The procedure must not change intervals after one event.
- The procedure must record the old interval and the change date for each update.

For each vehicle, the documentation must show cost per mile, downtime hours, and mean time between failures. Management can compare these values to balance cost and reliability.

The key sections for CQRS internal documentation are as follows:

1. Overview
This section defines CQRS. It states the system purpose. It identifies the audience and the required prior knowledge.

2. Architecture
This section shows the read model and the write model. It lists the data stores and the message infrastructure.

3. Commands and command handlers
This section explains command validation and write-side workflow. It gives the location of the code and the command API.

4. Queries and read models
This section explains the read-side data sources. It lists each projection and its source events.

5. Event flow and synchronization
This section explains how writes become reads. It describes the transport, the ordering, and the retry policy.

6. Consistency and failure behavior
This section states the consistency guarantee. It defines the lag between write and read. It lists failure recovery steps.

7. Development workflow
This section gives the rules for new commands and queries. It includes testing requirements and code review checks.

8. Deployment and configuration
This section lists environment variables and deployment order. It includes rollback steps.

9. Operations and diagnostic queries
This section lists alerts and common failure modes. It gives diagnostic queries for each model.

10. Known limitations and trade-offs
This section records the accepted costs. It links each cost to the benefit it buys.

The trade-off explanation has a separate paragraph for each trade-off. The benefit appears first. Then the cost appears.

Benefit: You can scale the read side and the write side independently.
Cost: You must maintain two models and the synchronization code.

Benefit: You can optimize read queries without affecting the command path.
Cost: The read model is not the system of record. The write model remains the source of truth.

Benefit: You can give each model a schema that matches its usage.
Cost: You duplicate some data between the models.

Benefit: You can serve reads from a store that is optimized for queries.
Cost: The read model lags behind the write model. The lag duration depends on the transport and the load.

Benefit: You can replay events to rebuild a read projection.
Cost: Event replay can require a long time for large histories.

Benefit: You can audit writes through the command log.
Cost: The command log and the event log increase storage and operational work.

Documenters must not claim that CQRS removes all read-write contention. It separates the models but does not remove the underlying database load.

A schema migration is a controlled change to the structure of a database. It can add, change, or remove tables, columns, indexes, and constraints. It can also change data.

The application must continue to read and write data during the change. The safe method is the expand-contract pattern. The database and the application pass through compatible intermediate states. Some changes require a short maintenance window. The exact procedure depends on your database system and workload. A zero-downtime migration is not always possible.

Safe procedure

Before you change a schema, do these steps.

1. Put the current schema in version control.
2. Back up the database.
3. Verify that the backup can be restored.
4. Test the rollback procedure in a separate environment.

Then follow these steps for the change.

1. Identify the required change.
2. Verify that the change is backward compatible.
3. If the change is backward compatible, apply the migration to the database.
4. If the change is not backward compatible, use the expand-contract procedure.
   - Add new tables, columns, or indexes.
   - Do not remove old objects.
   - Change the application to write to both the old and the new objects.
   - Fill data from the old objects into the new objects in small batches.
   - Verify that the new data matches the old data.
   - Deploy the application code that reads from the new objects.
   - Monitor application logs and database metrics.
   - Remove the old objects after a safe period.
5. If the migration fails, restore the backup.

Typical pitfalls and how to avoid them

- A long lock can stop writes. Use online DDL where the database supports it. Split large changes into batches.
- The application can read a schema that does not exist. Use the expand-contract pattern. Deploy schema changes before code that depends on them.
- A failed migration can leave a database in an unknown state. Make each migration script idempotent. Use a migration tool that records applied versions.
- Data loss can occur when you drop a column. Keep the old column until no code reads it. Back up data before the change.
- Implicit defaults can fill new columns with unexpected values. Set explicit defaults or nullable columns. Fill values before you add a not-null constraint.
- Foreign key constraints can block a table change. Create new tables without locks where possible. Use a shadow table for large changes.

Warnings

- Do not run migration scripts directly against production. The scripts can change or delete data.
- Do not apply a non-backward-compatible change while the old application version runs. The old code fails.

The guide can document four categories of feedback: formative, summative, immediate, and delayed. Different teaching systems use other categories. This answer covers these four common types.

Formative feedback

This feedback occurs while a student learns. It helps the student improve before a final assessment.

Examples:
- Comments on a draft essay that identify strengths and areas to improve.
- Questions that ask a student to explain a math solution.
- A quick quiz that shows which concepts the student did not learn.

Summative feedback

This feedback occurs after the lesson ends. It measures final achievement.

Examples:
- A final grade for a term paper.
- A score on a standardized test.
- A certificate that confirms completion of a course.

Immediate feedback

This feedback occurs at the same time as the student responds. It lets the student correct errors quickly.

Examples:
- A verbal correction during a class presentation.
- A red underline in a spelling app.
- A teacher confirms a correct answer during class.

Delayed feedback

This feedback occurs after a time delay. It lets the student reflect on the work.

Examples:
- Written comments that the teacher returns one week after a test.
- An audio note that the teacher sends after class.
- An online grade that appears after the teacher reads all essays.

Each school can adjust these examples to fit its system. The examples are common practice, not formal rules.

COMMON CAUSES

A home inkjet printer uses ink cartridges. It does not use toner.

Common causes are:
- The printer is offline or not connected.
- The printer driver is not present, damaged, or not set as the default printer.
- An ink cartridge is empty, clogged, or not installed correctly.
- A print job is stuck in the queue.
- A paper jam blocks the paper path.
- The printer or the computer needs a restart.

PROCEDURE

Do these steps in sequence. Stop when the printer prints again.

CONNECTIONS
1. Set the printer power switch to On.
2. Connect the USB cable firmly to the printer and the computer.
3. If the printer uses Wi-Fi, connect the printer and the computer to the same network.

PRINT QUEUE
4. Open the print queue on the computer.
5. Delete any stuck print jobs.
6. Set the printer status to Online.
7. If the queue does not clear, restart the printer and the computer.

DRIVER
8. Open the list of printers on the computer.
9. Find the printer model.
10. If the printer driver is not present or has an error, install the driver from the manufacturer website.
11. Set the printer as the default printer.

INK
12. Check the ink levels on the printer control panel or in the printer utility.
13. Replace any empty cartridge.
14. If the ink levels are sufficient, run a nozzle check.
15. If the nozzle check shows gaps, clean the print head.
16. Do not clean the print head more than three times. This process uses ink.

PAPER
17. Open the printer cover and the paper trays.
18. Remove all jammed paper gently.
19. Do not pull jammed paper with force. This action can damage the printer.
20. Close all covers.
21. Reload the paper tray.

ERROR MESSAGES
22. Read any error message on the printer display or the computer screen.
23. Follow the instructions in the message.
24. If the message is not clear, refer to the printer manual.

FINAL CHECK
25. If the printer still does not print, contact the printer manufacturer.

No, that claim is not true for all projects. Project managers often state this rule, but real project outcomes depend on context. Some successful projects start development with incomplete written specifications. These projects use iterative methods and regular customer feedback. Other projects, such as safety-critical systems, need more complete specifications before development. The claim overstates the role of written requirements.

A written specification does not guarantee that the project will succeed. Even a complete specification can contain ambiguous or conflicting requirements. Development often reveals new information that changes the initial requirements. For large systems, no single document can predict every interaction and failure mode. Requirements can change because of new laws, new market conditions, or new technical discoveries. Thus the absence of a full written specification is not a direct cause of failure.

In modern practice, clear requirements do not depend on a single static document. A clear requirement states one observable behavior or property that the system must have. It includes acceptance criteria that a team can verify with tests or demonstrations. It has a unique identifier and a traceable link to a stakeholder need. Teams write requirements incrementally for large or changeable systems. They refine the requirements after each iteration or after each user feedback session.

Large systems need more structure than small projects. Teams cannot write all requirements at the start because the system architecture is not yet stable. They use a requirements repository or a model to manage changes. They assign each requirement to a subsystem and to a release. They review new or changed requirements through a formal change control process. This approach keeps requirements clear without the need for a complete upfront specification.

Some domains, such as aviation or medical devices, demand a complete specification before development. In these domains, the law or a contract often requires the written specification. This does not mean that the specification alone ensures success. The team must still verify the design and the implementation against the specification.

In PostgreSQL, an UPDATE creates a new tuple and leaves the old tuple in the heap. A DELETE marks the existing tuple as deleted. A tuple becomes dead when no active transaction can read that version. Usually this occurs after the transaction that updated or deleted the row commits. If an older snapshot can still see the old version, the tuple is not dead yet. The tuple becomes dead after the transaction that holds that snapshot ends.

Sequential scans read all heap pages. The scan checks visibility for each tuple. Dead tuples use space in heap pages and increase I/O. The scan skips dead tuples after the visibility check. The table grows until vacuum removes the dead tuples. This growth degrades sequential scan performance.

Index scans use index entries that point to heap tuples, and these entries remain after the heap tuple becomes dead. The scan fetches the heap tuple and applies visibility checks. If the tuple is dead, the scan discards it. Index-only scans use the visibility map to avoid heap fetches. The visibility map cannot mark a page as all-visible when the page has a dead tuple. An index-only scan must visit the heap page for that tuple.

PostgreSQL uses the oldest active snapshot to decide which dead tuples vacuum can remove. A transaction that holds an old snapshot prevents the removal of tuples that the snapshot can see. Read-only transactions that run for a long time can hold such a snapshot. Prepared transactions also block tuple removal. A standby server with hot_standby_feedback can report a minimum transaction ID. These states cause dead tuple accumulation even when autovacuum runs.

Autovacuum starts a vacuum operation for a table when the number of dead tuples exceeds a threshold. The threshold equals autovacuum_vacuum_threshold plus autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor times the estimated number of live tuples. The defaults are 50 and 0.2. A snapshot that stays active for a long time can prevent the removal of many dead tuples. In that case, autovacuum still triggers but cannot reclaim space. Repeated vacuum runs can occur without a reduction in table size.

The old_snapshot_threshold setting controls an upper limit on snapshot age. When this limit is active, vacuum can remove tuples that older snapshots need. Transactions with such snapshots receive an error.

Autoscaling adds or removes capacity after a metric crosses a threshold. It does not prevent a slowdown during a sudden burst. Specific limits and defaults vary by provider.

Common reasons

- The scale metric is not the bottleneck. CPU use can stay low while memory, thread pools, or downstream services saturate.
- The scale policy uses an average metric, which hides short peaks.
- The scale-out threshold is too high, so the metric must stay high for several evaluation periods before scaling starts.
- Cooldown and warm-up settings delay extra capacity, and new instances need time to start and pass health checks.
- The maximum capacity is too low, so the group cannot add instances beyond this limit.
- Health checks or load balancer registration can delay traffic to new instances.
- Account or region capacity limits can prevent the launch of new instances.
- Some instance types have burst credit limits. When the credits run out, the instances process requests more slowly.
- A downstream component, for example a database or cache, can be the real limit, and more web servers do not help.

Checklist

Before you start, collect metrics from a slowdown period. Use the cloud console or CLI to access the scaling history and metrics.

Do not change scaling settings during peak traffic. The change can cause rapid scale in and scale out.

1. Check the scaling history during the slowdown for failed activities or rejected launches.
2. Check the alarm state and evaluation periods for the scale policy.
3. Check the statistic for the metric that the policy uses.
4. Check the scale-out threshold value.
5. Compare the scale metric with other resource metrics during the slowdown.
6. Check the instance type for burst credit limits.
7. Check the maximum capacity setting.
8. Check the cooldown period and warm-up settings.
9. Check the load balancer health check settings, the registration delay, and the health check grace period for the autoscaling group.
10. Check the account limits for instances or vCPUs in the region.
11. Check downstream components during the same period.

## Summary

B-tree index slowdowns in PostgreSQL usually come from index bloat, physical fragmentation, or outdated planner statistics. Outdated statistics change the query plan, not the physical index. These causes can exist together.

## Diagnostic procedure

Replace the placeholders with your schema, table, index, and column names.

1. If the extension is not present, run this command as a user that can create extensions:

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgstattuple;
```

2. Run this query to check table-level vacuum and analyze status:

```sql
SELECT schemaname,
       relname,
       n_live_tup,
       n_dead_tup,
       n_mod_since_analyze,
       last_vacuum,
       last_autovacuum,
       last_analyze,
       last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE schemaname = '<schema_name>'
  AND relname = '<table_name>';
```

3. Run this query outside peak hours to check the physical state of the index:

```sql
SELECT * FROM pgstatindex('<schema_name>.<index_name>');
```

4. Run this query to check column statistics for the filtered column:

```sql
SELECT attname,
       n_distinct,
       null_frac,
       correlation
FROM pg_stats
WHERE schemaname = '<schema_name>'
  AND tablename = '<table_name>'
  AND attname = '<column_name>';
```

5. Run this query to compare index usage counters:

```sql
SELECT relname,
       seq_scan,
       seq_tup_read,
       idx_scan,
       idx_tup_fetch
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE schemaname = '<schema_name>'
  AND relname = '<table_name>';
```

6. Run the slow query with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) to check the chosen plan.

## Interpretation guide

A high `n_dead_tup` value relative to `n_live_tup` indicates bloat. An old `last_analyze` timestamp or a high `n_mod_since_analyze` value indicates outdated statistics. These counter values are planner estimates, not exact counts.

A high `leaf_fragmentation` value indicates physical disorder. A low `avg_leaf_density` value indicates sparse pages. A low fillfactor also causes this state.

A `correlation` value near zero means that table row order does not match column order. This state can cause the planner to prefer a sequential scan.

If `seq_scan` increased while `idx_scan` did not increase after the slowdown, a plan change is likely. Compare the counters with a baseline from before the slowdown. There is no universal threshold.

Use these rules to decide the primary cause:

- Bloat is likely when `n_dead_tup` is high and `avg_leaf_density` is low.
- Fragmentation is likely when `leaf_fragmentation` is high.
- Outdated statistics are likely when `n_mod_since_analyze` is high or `last_analyze` is old and the plan changed.
- If all values are normal but the query is slower, check lock contention, storage latency, hardware changes, or PostgreSQL configuration changes.

These causes can overlap. Repeat the checks after a maintenance operation to separate them.

The first European presses from about 1450 had a wooden frame, a wooden screw, and a flat platen. Records from the first decades are incomplete. Later printer manuals such as Moxon's Mechanick Exercises (1683) describe common failures and repairs. These practices probably developed in the first decades.

The wooden screw threads wore quickly. Worn threads caused uneven pressure on the type. Printers replaced wooden threads with metal threads. They also made the platen larger and flatter. These changes gave a more even impression across the page.

The wooden frame flexed under the force of the screw. A flexed frame produced a weak print at the edges. Printers added iron braces to the frame. Later press builders made the frame from iron. This change reduced flex.

Metal type wore at the shoulders and the face. Worn type gave broken or thin letters. Printers cast type from a harder alloy of lead, tin, and antimony. They kept spare letters for the most common sorts. This practice reduced downtime for recasting.

The ink was thick. It clogged the type and transferred unevenly. Pressmen used leather ink balls to dab the ink onto the type. They kept a thin, even film of ink on the balls. They cleaned the balls after each work period.

Paper had to be damp before a print run. Dry paper resisted the ink. Pressmen stored sheets between wet felt cloths. This method kept the paper pliable. It allowed a clean transfer of ink.

The sheet shifted on the tympan during the pull. A shifted sheet caused a doubled image. Pressmen fixed the sheet with two sharp points on the tympan. They used a frisket to hold the paper and to cover blank areas. These tools made register more reliable.

Pressmen applied tallow or soap to the screw threads. The lubricant reduced friction and wear. They inspected the press before each work day. A broken part stopped production. Printers kept spare wooden parts for quick repair.

These practices varied by workshop and by region. No single design was standard in the first decades.

Fully worked examples present all solution steps. Faded examples present some steps and omit others. For learners with substantial domain knowledge, fully worked examples often contain redundant information. This redundancy can increase extraneous cognitive load. Faded examples require these learners to retrieve the omitted steps. That retrieval supports schema automation and transfer to new problems.

Common findings show the expertise reversal effect. Guidance that helps novices can reduce learning for learners with experience. Fully worked examples are high-guidance materials. They can slow down knowledgeable learners and reduce practice. In contrast, faded examples balance guidance and active solution attempts. Many controlled studies report better transfer after faded examples for these learners.

The benefits of faded examples reverse under these conditions:

- High element interactivity. The task has many parts that interact. Full worked examples often manage working memory load better than faded examples for these tasks.
- Early or excessive fading. If fading removes steps before the learner has enough practice, error rates increase. The learner must then recover with extra effort.
- Nonuniform prior knowledge. If a learner knows some subtasks but not others, uniform fading causes errors on unfamiliar subtasks. Adaptive fading can prevent this reversal.

Caulk is a flexible material that fills gaps and seals joints.

Silicone caulk is made from silicone polymers. It cures to a rubber-like solid. It stays flexible after it cures. It resists water and mildew. It sticks well to smooth non-porous surfaces. Silicone caulk is not paintable.

Acrylic caulk is made from water-based acrylic resin. It dries to a paintable solid. It is easier to apply than silicone caulk. It cleans with water before it cures. It sticks well to wood and drywall, but it is less flexible than silicone caulk. It can shrink and crack in wet areas.

For a bathtub, silicone caulk is the correct choice. The joint around a tub must stay watertight. The tub moves slightly when it fills with water. Silicone caulk remains flexible and resists mold. Acrylic caulk will fail sooner in this wet location.

For a kitchen countertop, the decision depends on the location of the joint. Around the sink and along the backsplash, silicone caulk is the correct choice. These areas get splashes and cleaning water. Acrylic caulk is suitable only for dry joints that require paint. If the caulk must match a painted wall, acrylic caulk is an option only in dry areas.

Tires need a specific pressure, and the air pressure supports the vehicle load.
It keeps the tire contact patch at the correct shape and size.
That shape gives the best traction and the shortest stop.
It also gives the best vehicle control.
The recommended pressure also balances fuel economy and tire wear.
A tire below or above that pressure cannot do its job correctly.

Too low pressure causes problems.
The sidewalls flex too much.
Too much flex creates heat.
Too much heat can cause a sudden air loss or tread separation.
The tire also wears faster on both edges.
Low pressure increases fuel consumption and makes the vehicle respond more slowly.

Too high pressure causes different problems.
The contact patch becomes smaller and rounder.
The center of the tread carries most of the load.
The tire wears faster in the center.
A smaller contact patch reduces traction and increases the distance to stop.
The ride becomes harsh, and the tire can suffer impact damage.

Air pressure changes with temperature.
The pressure increases when the tires get warm.
The pressure decreases when the tires get cold.
A common estimate is about 1 psi for each 10 degrees Fahrenheit of temperature change.
The vehicle manufacturer specifies the cold inflation pressure as the value to check before the vehicle moves for the first time that day.
If you release air from a warm tire to reach the cold pressure, the tire is underinflated after it cools.

Distributed tracing records the path of a request as it moves through services in a microservices environment. Each service creates a span that describes one unit of work and includes the service name. A trace is a set of spans that share one trace ID. One service starts the trace and adds the trace ID to outgoing requests. Each downstream service reads the trace ID and creates a child span. A span records its duration and an error status.

Instrumentation adds code that creates spans and propagates context. Manual instrumentation uses a tracing library in each service. Automatic instrumentation adds tracing to common libraries without changes to application code. Each added span gives more detail but uses CPU and memory. It also uses network bandwidth when the span is exported. You can start with coarse spans for service calls and add spans for critical operations only.

Head-based sampling decides at the start of a request whether to record the trace. The service often selects a fixed percentage of traces, such as 1 percent. For an unsampled trace, services can skip span creation. This method limits overhead and is simple to operate. It can miss rare errors or slow traces that do not fall in the sampled fraction. A change in the sample rate changes the data volume and the chance to see rare events.

Tail-based sampling decides after all spans in a trace complete. The tracing system holds spans in a buffer or a queue until the decision. It can keep all traces that contain an error or exceed a latency threshold. This method gives better coverage for rare problems. It uses more memory and storage. It also uses more network bandwidth.

The best amount of instrumentation depends on your observability goals and your cost limits. You can start with coarse spans for service calls and add spans for critical operations only. A high-volume service can use head-based sampling with a low rate. Tail-based sampling is better for traces that must include errors, even if storage cost increases. You can measure the overhead of instrumentation before you increase the span count. The exact behavior varies by tracing vendor and runtime.

A higher MERV rating does not always mean better indoor air quality. A higher MERV filter traps more small particles, but it also creates more resistance to airflow. Engineers call this resistance pressure drop. A filter with a high pressure drop can reduce airflow or increase fan energy use. Reduced airflow can cause the evaporator coil to freeze in cooling mode. Reduced airflow can also cause the furnace heat exchanger to overheat.

The correct MERV rating depends on the system. The manufacturer specification states the maximum MERV rating and the maximum pressure drop for the system. Some residential systems accept MERV 13 filters. Many others require a lower MERV rating. A filter within the manufacturer specification provides filtration without excessive airflow resistance.

A connection pool maintains a set of open database connections. Applications borrow a connection from the pool when they need database access. When an application finishes with a connection, it returns the connection to the pool. The pool lends that connection to a later request. This reuse removes the cost of a new network handshake and authentication for every request.

Without a pool, each database operation opens a new connection. That action requires a network handshake, authentication, and memory allocation on the client and server. These tasks take time and resources. Under heavy load, many short-lived connections can exhaust database connection limits. A pool keeps a bounded set of connections open. This approach reduces connection setup overhead and limits concurrent server connections.

These common configuration parameters control a connection pool:

- Maximum pool size: the largest number of connections that the pool will create and hold.
- Minimum pool size: the number of connections that the pool keeps open when traffic is low.
- Connection timeout: the time that an application will wait for a connection before the request fails.
- Idle timeout: the time after which the pool closes a connection that has no activity.
- Connection test query: a query that the pool runs before it lends a connection. The result verifies that the connection is still valid.

Exact parameter names and defaults differ by database driver and library.

X-Frame-Options is a response header. It tells the browser to block the page from appearing in an iframe, frame, embed, or object. The header supports two modern values: DENY and SAMEORIGIN. DENY blocks the page in all frames. SAMEORIGIN allows framing only when the top-level page has the same origin as the framed page. The legacy value ALLOW-FROM specifies a single permitted origin, but major browsers now ignore it.

This guarantee applies only to browsers that enforce the header. Old browsers, such as early Internet Explorer versions, do not enforce the header. Text-only or embedded browsers can also ignore it. The header does not provide a server-side check. It does not block other clickjacking methods that use pop-up windows or separate tabs.

In modern browsers, CSP frame-ancestors takes precedence over X-Frame-Options when both are present. This means X-Frame-Options alone can be less strict than the CSP policy. If a CSP frame-ancestors directive allows a specific sequence of ancestors, the page can load in a frame. The X-Frame-Options value is then not enforced.

For nested frames, SAMEORIGIN checks the top-level origin. A cross-origin intermediate frame cannot bypass this check. But if the top-level origin matches, nested frames can still present content on top of the page. The header does not prevent clickjacking within the same origin. A same-origin page can overlay another same-origin page without violating the header.

Common causes:

1. Git prevents the same branch from being checked out in more than one worktree. That error occurs when you add a worktree for an already-used branch.
2. A lock file exists in the worktree metadata directory. This file is `.git/worktrees/<name>/locked`. An interrupted command or a manual lock creates it.
3. A stale `index.lock` file exists in the worktree's git directory. A previous Git process did not remove it.
4. The target directory for the new worktree is not empty. Or the path is inside the main working tree.
5. The repository is bare and the worktree configuration is incomplete. Or you run the command from the wrong repository.

Diagnosis and resolution:

1. Run `git worktree list` to show all worktrees and their branches.
2. Run `git worktree list --porcelain` to show lock information.
3. If a worktree shows a `locked` entry, verify that no Git process uses that worktree.
4. Run `git worktree unlock <path>` to remove the lock.
5. For a branch already checked out, add the worktree with a new branch. Use: `git worktree add -b <new-branch> <path> <base>`.
6. If you must use the same branch in another location, use detached HEAD. Use: `git worktree add --detach <path>`.
7. If a stale `index.lock` file exists, verify that no Git process runs in that worktree. Remove the stale `index.lock` file.
8. Run `git worktree prune --dry-run` to list stale worktree metadata.
9. Run `git worktree prune` to remove stale metadata.

Internal management escalation is a request to leaders inside your company. Vendor support escalation is a request to the external vendor that supplies a product or service. Both paths ask for more attention to an unresolved customer issue. The difference is who receives the request.

For a small support team, three decision points matter.

- Cause location. If the issue comes from the team's own configuration, code, or process, the correct path is internal management escalation. If the issue comes from the vendor product or service, the correct path is vendor support escalation.
- Isolation status. If the cause is unknown, the team must isolate the problem before it picks a path. Basic checks can separate an internal fault from a vendor fault. Without this separation, the wrong path wastes time.
- Contract and customer risk. Vendor escalation can require a paid support contract with defined severity levels. Internal escalation can still be necessary for a vendor issue if the team must manage customer communications or get budget approval. The team must check the support contract and the customer impact before escalation.

The two paths are not exclusive. A team can escalate internally and to the vendor at the same time when both resource and product issues exist.

In preliminary design, engineers use a simple nut factor model to estimate clamp force from applied torque. The model is T = K D F. T is applied torque, K is nut factor, D is nominal thread diameter, and F is clamp force. The nut factor combines thread friction, underhead friction, and thread geometry into one value. This model is common for early design before detailed tests.

A more accurate relation separates three torque components: thread pitch work, thread friction work, and underhead friction work.
T = F × [ p/(2π) + μ_t r_t / cos β + μ_b r_b ]
Here, p is thread pitch, β is thread flank angle, and r_t and r_b are effective radii. μ_t is thread friction coefficient, and μ_b is underhead friction coefficient. Lubrication reduces both friction coefficients and can make them more constant. This equation shows that friction terms consume most torque, while only the pitch term creates preload.

Workflow for preliminary estimate:
- The engineer sets a target clamp force from the joint load, safety factor, and embedment loss.
- The engineer selects the fastener size, strength class, and material.
- The engineer estimates thread friction and underhead friction from the surface finish, coating, and lubricant.
- The engineer calculates the required torque with the nut factor model or the detailed formula.
- The engineer performs torque-tension tests on sample joints to calibrate the nut factor for the actual batch.
- The engineer checks the preload with a statistical tolerance or direct measurement for critical joints.

The nut factor K is not a material property. It depends on friction and surface condition. For common steel fasteners, K often ranges from 0.10 to 0.25. Even with the same torque, scatter in friction causes clamp force variation of ±25 percent to ±35 percent. A common rule of thumb splits torque as 50 percent underhead friction, 40 percent thread friction, and 10 percent axial preload. This split shows that small friction changes produce large preload errors, so torque control alone gives uncertain preload.

Generic torque-preload data applies only to the exact combination of fastener, coating, lubricant, material, and temperature. A generic conversion cannot guarantee preload for safety-critical joints. Engineers must use joint-specific torque specifications when preload affects fatigue life, leak tightness, or load capacity. Engineers must use direct preload measurement for joints with high consequence of failure, such as pressure vessels, engine cylinder heads, and structural connections. Direct measurement methods include strain gauges, ultrasonic bolt stretch, and washer-type load cells. These methods remove friction uncertainty because they measure axial force directly or controlled elongation.

Run these checks in a local clone. The commands are read-only.

1. Run `git fetch --all --prune`.
2. Compare local and remote develop: `git rev-parse develop origin/develop`.
3. Find the branch point of release: `git merge-base develop release`.
4. Show the commit history for each changed file on develop: `git log --oneline develop -- path/to/file1 path/to/file2`.
5. Show the same history on release: `git log --oneline release -- path/to/file1 path/to/file2`.
6. Identify the last commit that touched each file on develop: `git log -1 --format="%H %ci %s" develop -- path/to/file1`.
7. Identify the same on release: `git log -1 --format="%H %ci %s" release -- path/to/file1`.
8. Show all parents of the squash merge commit: `git cat-file -p <squash-merge-sha>`.
   A squash merge commit has one parent. A regular merge commit has two parents.
9. Search for revert commits after the merge: `git log --oneline --grep='revert' develop`.
10. Show the graph around the merge: `git log --graph --oneline --decorate develop --not release`.
11. Compare file contents between the two branches: `git diff develop release -- path/to/file1 path/to/file2`.
12. Inspect branch protection settings in the repository UI.
    Look for the setting named 'Require branches to be up to date before merging'.

Interpret the results:
- If step 4 does not show the feature merge commit, the commit is not on develop.
- If step 5 shows the commit but the file content is old, a later commit changed the files.
- If step 3 shows an old merge base, release was created from an old develop commit.
- If step 2 shows different commit hashes, local refs are stale. Use `origin/develop` everywhere.
- If branch protection does not require up-to-date branches, a later merge into release can reintroduce old file versions.

This answer compares flexible intermediate bulk containers (FIBCs) with rigid composite IBCs for hygroscopic powders in intermodal freight. The comparison covers high-humidity transshipment points and rail and truck vibration. The focus is moisture ingress, stacking limits, discharge completeness, and reusability trade-offs. Performance depends on the container design, liner material, closure method, and operational practices.

A rigid composite IBC usually gives better protection against moisture ingress than a standard FIBC. The rigid plastic bottle and screw closure form a seal that resists humid air and liquid water. A FIBC fabric is not a moisture barrier. A FIBC needs a separate liner with heat-sealed or tied closures. High humidity and vibration can cause condensation and loosen tied FIBC closures more easily than screw caps. A FIBC with a high-barrier liner and sealed spouts can approach the same protection, but closure integrity is harder to maintain.

Rigid composite IBCs have a structural frame, so they can support vertical loads from other containers in a stack. The maximum stack height depends on the design, the product weight, and the UN or manufacturer rating. Many rigid composite IBCs are rated for two units high, and some designs permit three or four units high with a compatible base. FIBCs have no rigid frame, so their sidewalls can bulge and shift under load. A stack of FIBCs more than two high is usually not recommended, and some FIBC designs do not allow a stack. Rail and truck vibration increases the risk of a stack collapse for FIBCs more than for rigid composite IBCs.

A FIBC with a bottom spout can discharge almost all product if an operator lifts and massages the bag. Residue can remain in the seams, corners, and liner creases. A rigid composite IBC discharges through a bottom outlet valve. The discharge completeness depends on the bottle floor shape, the outlet position, and the powder flow. Some rigid composite IBCs have a sloped sump that assists complete discharge. Flat-bottom rigid IBCs with a raised outlet can hold back more product and can require a tilt or a special discharge station.

FIBCs are often single-trip containers because the fabric, liner, and sling loops degrade with use and exposure. Reuse of a FIBC requires inspection for cuts, abrasion, moisture uptake, and loss of static or UN certification. A reusable FIBC must have a design, marking, and test history that supports the intended number of trips. Rigid composite IBCs are usually designed for multiple uses. Users can reuse the outer frame and pallet and can clean or replace the inner bottle. Reuse of rigid composite IBCs requires reverse logistics, cleanliness validation, and inspection of closures and valves.

This comparison covers npm package-lock.json with lockfileVersion 2 and Yarn v1 yarn.lock in a monorepo. It applies to npm version 7 or later and Yarn version 1.22. This comparison does not cover Yarn version 2 or later. Behavior can vary by minor version and package metadata.

For determinism, both formats pin exact versions, resolved URLs, and integrity hashes. npm lockfileVersion 2 adds a packages section that records the installed tree. That section records hoisted paths and workspace packages. Yarn v1 yarn.lock records versions per dependency selector but does not record the final hoisted tree. Both formats record platform-specific optional packages, and installers skip packages that do not match the current platform. Yarn v1 keeps one root yarn.lock for all workspaces.

For conflict resolution, npm version 7 and later treat peer dependencies as required. npm can stop installation with ERESOLVE errors when peer dependencies conflict, and lockfileVersion 2 records peer dependencies and peerDependenciesMeta. Yarn v1 does not enforce peer dependency conflicts in the same way. Yarn v1 does not install missing peer dependencies automatically, and it prints warnings for missing or incompatible peer dependencies. For optional platform-specific packages, both tools check the os and cpu fields. Both tools can skip optional packages that do not match the current platform, and optional package install failures usually do not stop the install.

Migration from npm to Yarn v1 has these trade-offs.
- Yarn v1 does not use package-lock.json as a lockfile, so you must generate a new yarn.lock from package.json.
- The dependency graph can change because resolution and layout algorithms differ.
- Peer dependency errors become warnings, and missing or incompatible peers can remain undetected.
- Optional packages for another operating system or CPU can appear in the lockfile but will not install on the CI platform.
- CI caches keyed on package-lock.json become invalid, and a new yarn.lock changes cache keys.
- Monorepo workspace dependency placement differs, and installed dependency trees can differ after migration.

No single migration step preserves every dependency decision. A review of the new lockfile and tests for all platform-specific packages are necessary before CI use.

Use a lock file that contains exact versions. Use one file for pip dependencies, for example `requirements.lock` generated by `pip-tools` or `poetry.lock`. Cache the pip download cache and the pre-commit environment cache.

Set the cache key from the lock file and the pre-commit configuration file. The key changes when either file changes. This prevents stale caches.

Example `.gitlab-ci.yml`:
```yaml
variables:
  PIP_CACHE_DIR: $CI_PROJECT_DIR/.cache/pip
  PRE_COMMIT_HOME: $CI_PROJECT_DIR/.cache/pre-commit

cache:
  key:
    prefix: v1
    files:
      - requirements.lock
      - .pre-commit-config.yaml
  paths:
    - .cache/pip
    - .cache/pre-commit
  policy: pull-push

install:
  script:
    - pip install -r requirements.lock
    - pip install pre-commit
    - pre-commit run --all-files
```

Runner configuration:
Use a distributed cache. Set the cache storage in the runner `config.toml` to an S3-compatible object store or GCS. A local cache on one runner does not share across runners.

```toml
[runners.cache]
  Type = 's3'
  Shared = true
  [runners.cache.s3]
    ServerAddress = 's3.amazonaws.com'
    AccessKey = 'MY_ACCESS_KEY'
    SecretKey = 'MY_SECRET_KEY'
    BucketName = 'my-cache-bucket'
```

Fallback steps:
1. If no cache exists for the key, the install step rebuilds the dependencies. Do not fail the job. This is the expected fallback.
2. If the lock files change, the key changes. The next pipeline does not restore the old cache.
3. If you need a clean build, add a version number to the cache key prefix and increment it.

Use one cache key design for the whole project. Do not mix a file-based key with a static key for the same paths.

A document template gives the structure and wording for a type of document. It contains fixed text and placeholders for variable text. The placeholders are completed to make a specific document.

An example is one completed document. It shows one possible result, but it does not show which parts are fixed. A single example does not identify the fixed parts.

A boilerplate paragraph is fixed text that is used without changes. A template can include one or more boilerplate paragraphs. A template also includes fields that change for each use. Thus a boilerplate paragraph can be a part of a template, but a template is more than boilerplate text.

Dear [Customer Name],

Regards,
[Agent Name]

The governing welding code determines which variables are essential and which are nonessential. If you use ASME BPVC Section IX, refer to QW-252 for GTAW essential variables and QW-253 for nonessential variables. Other codes, such as AWS D1.6, use different lists. Confirm the applicable code before you start.

Administrative data
- WPS number: ________
- Date: ________
- Welding process: GTAW
- Supporting PQR number: ________
- Governing code and edition: ________
- Base metal specification and P-number or group number: ________
- Base metal thickness range qualified: ________
- Filler metal specification, classification, and A-number: ________
- Shielding gas type and flow rate: ________
- Backing gas type and flow rate: ________
- Joint design reference or sketch number: ________

Essential variables
The list below shows common categories. Confirm the complete list in your governing code.

Hygienic requirements for dairy pipe
Stainless steel pipe in a dairy facility usually requires a smooth, crevice-free internal weld surface. The facility can require a full penetration joint and internal purge to prevent oxidation. Record the acceptance criteria for undercut, reinforcement, and surface finish. Obtain these criteria from the owner and from the applicable sanitary standard.

- If the work is in a confined space, test the atmosphere for oxygen and argon before entry.

- AWS D1.6/D1.6M, Structural Welding Code - Stainless Steel, if applicable

Records to attach

- Supporting PQR

- Calibration certificates for welding equipment
