The authorization server performs the enforcement. If the value is an empty array, no scopes are listed for that scheme. For API key and mutual TLS schemes, the value does not define scopes. The presence of the scheme in the object still requires the credential or certificate.

A single Security Requirement Object can combine multiple scheme types. For example, the object `api_key: [], oauth2: [ "read:things" ], mutualTLS: []` requires the API key, the OAuth2 scope, and the client certificate. Separate objects in the array give alternatives. The array `security: [ { api_key: [] }, { oauth2: [ "read:things" ], mutualTLS: [] } ]` has two alternatives. The first permits the API key alone. The second permits OAuth2 and mutual TLS together.

The OpenAPI Specification defines the empty array as a removal instruction only for the Operation Object. For the root OpenAPI Object, an empty array declares no security requirements. The specification does not assign a removal effect there. Tool behavior can vary.

An embedding is a fixed-length vector of real numbers. It represents an object, such as a word, an image, or a user. Similar objects have vectors that are close in the vector space. This closeness is measured by cosine similarity, dot product, or Euclidean distance.

Text embeddings represent meaning and usage. Word embeddings, for example word2vec or GloVe, place words with similar contexts near each other. Sentence embeddings from transformer models map a whole sentence to one vector. They are usually trained with masked word prediction or with a contrastive objective for similar and different sentences. The result depends on the model and the text used for training. Text embeddings often use cosine similarity because vector direction is more important than vector length.

Image embeddings represent visual features. Convolutional networks and vision transformers produce image vectors. Early layers capture edges and textures. Final layers capture objects and scenes. A model trained for image classification can produce a vector before the output layer. That vector often contains class-related information but can lose fine detail.

Recommendation embeddings put users and items in the same vector space. A user vector is close to items that the user has liked. New users or items with no interactions have poor embeddings. This is the cold-start problem.

Supervised learning uses labels. For example, an image model can learn to classify animals. The layer before the output then becomes the image embedding. Self-supervised learning uses the data itself. For text, a model can predict the next word. For images, a positive pair is two views of the same image.

Collaborative filtering uses only interactions. Matrix factorization finds user and item vectors that predict ratings or rankings. Two-tower neural networks are a common deep method. Multimodal contrastive learning uses paired text and images. It pulls a text-image pair together when the pair is related. It pushes other pairs apart.

Several properties make an embedding useful:

- The similarity structure must match the task. For search, relevant items must be closer to the query than irrelevant items.
- Invariance must match the noise in the data. Useful text embeddings ignore changes in words that do not change meaning.
- Sensitivity must keep the signals that matter. The word not must change the sentence vector.
- Dimension affects capacity and cost. A low dimension can lose distinctions. A high dimension can increase storage and retrieval cost.
- The metric must match the objective that the model optimized. If a model was optimized with cosine similarity, cosine similarity is the usual metric for search.
- Coverage affects performance. Embeddings reflect the data used for training. If the data does not cover a domain, results will degrade.
- For cross-modal search, embeddings must share one vector space. Text and image vectors must be aligned.
- For classification, useful embeddings often separate classes with a simple boundary.

No embedding is universally better. The best choice depends on the task, the data, and the model. Different models produce different geometry. A distance threshold that works for one model can fail for another. The target task provides the relevant quality measure.

Cognitive Load Types

- Intrinsic load is the inherent complexity of the content for a particular learner. It depends on element interactivity and on the learner's prior knowledge. A concept with many elements that interact, such as a regression model with interaction terms, has higher intrinsic load than a single mean. It decreases when the learner forms schemas.
- Extraneous load is the load that an instructional design adds without support for schema acquisition. Common sources are split attention, redundancy, and irrelevant details. This load consumes working memory but does not support schema acquisition.
- Germane load is the working memory resource that a learner directs to schema construction and automation. Instructors do not add germane load directly. They create conditions that free resources for it.

Interactions

Working memory has a limited capacity. The three load types compete for that capacity. The total load must stay below the limit of working memory capacity. High intrinsic load requires low extraneous load so that the learner can invest resources in germane processes. If a task has low intrinsic load, redundant instruction can still add extraneous load and reduce efficiency.

Task Sequence

A course must start with tasks that have low element interactivity and build to tasks that have high element interactivity. This order reduces intrinsic load before the learner attempts complex material. Each new concept must connect to schemas that the learner already holds.

Worked Examples

For novices, full worked examples reduce extraneous load. The examples must show problem states and solution steps in one integrated format. The instructor can ask learners to explain the steps to support germane processes. Completion problems follow full examples. Support decreases as the learner forms schemas.

Expertise Reversal Effect

Expertise reversal effect occurs when an instructional support that helps novices becomes extraneous for experts. Experts already hold schemas for the content, so the same material has lower intrinsic load for them. Redundant worked examples and split attention add extraneous load for experts. A course with mixed prior knowledge can use a pretest to assign paths. Novices receive full worked examples and completion problems. Experts receive problem tasks without redundant explanations.

API Error Format Reference

When to use RFC 7807 problem details

Problem details apply to HTTP APIs that return errors to clients. They apply when clients read error fields from responses. They apply when one error format must cover Node.js and Python services. The media type is application/problem+json. They do not apply to non-HTTP protocols.

Problem details fields

The standard fields are:
- type: identifies the error type.
- title: gives a short summary.
- status: gives the HTTP status code from the response.
- detail: gives a human-readable explanation.
- instance: identifies the specific error occurrence.
Extension members hold service-specific data for field errors, request IDs, and validation details.

Status code mapping

Malformed requests return 400 Bad Request. Requests with invalid field values return 422 Unprocessable Entity. Some teams return 400 for all validation errors. The 422 status is common but not required by RFC 7807. Server errors return 500 Internal Server Error. Responses must not expose stack traces or internal details.

Trade-offs

Custom envelope:
A custom envelope gives full control over the response shape. It requires each client to write a custom parser. It increases documentation and maintenance work. A custom envelope places arbitrary fields at the top level.

Standard type:
RFC 7807 is a standard type that uses a known media type. It allows general-purpose client libraries. It keeps non-standard data in extension members.

Recommendation:
RFC 7807 is suitable for new APIs that need interoperability. A custom envelope is suitable for contracts that already exist and require the old shape.

Safety Factor Selection for Static and Fatigue Load Conditions

This section gives rules for the selection of safety factors for static and fatigue load conditions. Use these rules for mechanical components in initial design and design review. The exact values come from the applicable design code or company standard. Do not use a value that is below the code minimum.

For static load conditions, the safety factor is the ratio of the material strength to the design stress. Use the minimum specified tensile or yield strength from the material standard. Account for material property uncertainty with a higher factor. Use a higher factor when the consequence of failure is severe.

For fatigue load conditions, use the endurance limit or fatigue strength at the required number of cycles. Correct the test data for surface finish, size, temperature, and reliability. Apply a fatigue safety factor to the stress amplitude. The factor must account for scatter in fatigue data. Scatter is larger for fatigue data than for static data.

Material property uncertainty is the difference between the test coupon and the actual component. The difference results from heat treatment, geometry, and production process. Use a higher safety factor when the material certificate is absent or incomplete. You can use a lower factor only when you have statistical data from the same batch and process.

The consequence of failure sets the minimum safety factor. Use a higher factor when failure can cause injury, loss of life, or major asset damage. Use a lower factor when failure causes only a controlled shutdown and small repair cost. The factor must increase with the severity of the consequence.

Inspection quality limits the largest defect that can remain in the component. A lower inspection quality requires a higher safety factor. The safety factor must cover the possible defect size that the inspection does not detect. Non-destructive inspection methods have detection limits. Use the detection limit from the procedure qualification.

A qualified engineer must verify the selected safety factors when one or more of these conditions are true:
- The component is safety-critical.
- The load condition includes fatigue or impact.
- The material data are limited.
- The inspection method is new or unproven.
- The operating environment changes.

The verification must include a review of all assumptions, load cases, and failure modes.

For a read-heavy SaaS, compare synchronous and asynchronous streaming replication on these axes: failover safety, read capacity, write latency, and practical trade-offs.

Failover safety

Synchronous replication makes the primary wait until a synchronous standby confirms WAL persistence before it returns from commit. With `synchronous_commit = remote_apply` or `on`, an acknowledged transaction survives primary failure if that standby remains available. This guarantee fails if the standby is lost with the primary. This setup gives a recovery point objective of zero for acknowledged commits. Asynchronous replication sends WAL to the standby, and the primary does not wait for standby confirmation. A primary crash can lose transactions that the standby did not receive, and the loss window equals the replication lag at that moment.

Read capacity

Both modes support read-only queries on a hot standby. Read queries require `hot_standby = on` on the standby. Synchronous and asynchronous replication both allow read replicas and query routing to them. The mode affects data recency on the replica, not the capacity for read traffic. An asynchronous replica can serve reads that lag the primary by seconds or minutes. A synchronous replica with `remote_apply` reduces this visible lag for newly acknowledged commits, but this benefit adds write latency.

Write latency

Asynchronous replication adds almost no latency to the primary write path. The primary writes WAL locally. It sends WAL to standbys without a wait for a reply. Network or standby disk speed can affect replication lag, but it does not delay commit acknowledgment.

Synchronous replication adds at least one network round trip to the standby. It also adds the time for the standby to flush WAL. With `remote_apply`, it adds the time for the standby to replay WAL. This latency depends on distance, network quality, and standby storage speed. In a single region, the added latency is usually small. Across regions, the added latency can be large enough to affect client writes.

Practical trade-offs

- Synchronous replication gives zero acknowledged data loss on failover if the synchronous standby survives. A failed sync standby can block all commits that require a sync acknowledgment.
- The `synchronous_standby_names` setting supports `ANY 1 (standby1, standby2)` to accept any one of two standbys. This setup continues writes if one standby remains available.
- A safe failover promotes a standby that was synchronous at the time of the primary failure.
- Asynchronous replication keeps write latency low and does not wait for standby confirmation. It accepts a data loss window on failover.
- A replication slot for an asynchronous standby prevents WAL removal on the primary before the standby receives it. A slot does not prevent loss from a crash that occurs before transmission.
- PostgreSQL streaming replication does not include automatic failover. A separate system must detect failure and promote a standby.
- A common design for read-heavy SaaS uses one synchronous standby for durability. Additional asynchronous standbys serve read queries.

Packet Capture for Intermittent Latency Troubleshooting

Capture Points
Three capture points provide the necessary views: the client, the server, and a network tap or mirror port between them. A tap gives a copy of all packets on the link. A switch mirror port can drop packets under load. A comparison of these captures localizes the delay.

Filters
A capture filter limits the capture to the endpoint IP addresses and the TCP or UDP ports for the application. A filter that includes only the client address can miss the return path. The return path from the server can differ. Display filters after capture identify these symptoms:
- TCP retransmissions
- duplicate acknowledgments
- zero window advertisements
- long gaps between packets

TLS Limitations
TLS encrypts the application data. The capture shows only the encrypted payload and the TLS record headers. A capture at the client or server sees the same encrypted bytes as a network tap. In TLS 1.2, the server certificate and the Server Name Indication are visible. In TLS 1.3, the server certificate is encrypted in the handshake. You can infer network-level latency from these observations:
- timestamps on packets
- round-trip times for TCP handshakes
- retransmissions
- packet spacing

You cannot infer application-level latency, server processing time, HTTP status codes, or payload contents.

Use this workflow for a small team with GitHub pull requests.

Prerequisites
1. Install Git.
2. Clone the repository.
3. Enable branch protection on the `main` branch.
4. Require pull request reviews before merge.
5. Require status checks to pass before merge.
6. Use one local clone per developer.

Feature branch workflow
1. Update your local `main` branch.
   Run `git checkout main`.
   Run `git pull`.
2. Create a feature branch from `main`.
   Run `git checkout -b feature/<short-name>`.
3. Make changes and commit them.
   Use small commits.
4. Push the feature branch.
   Run `git push -u origin feature/<short-name>`.
5. Open a pull request from the feature branch to `main`.
6. Request a review from one teammate.
7. Wait for the review and the required checks.
8. If the reviewer requests changes, apply them and push again.
9. Update the branch with the latest `main` before the merge.
   - If only you use the branch, run `git fetch origin` and `git rebase origin/main`.
   - If other developers use the branch, run `git fetch origin` and `git merge origin/main`.
10. Resolve conflicts locally.
    After you resolve a conflict, run `git add <file>` and `git commit`.
    Do not commit unresolved conflict markers.
11. Push the updated branch.
    After a rebase, run `git push --force-with-lease`.
    Do not use `git push --force`.
    After a merge, run `git push`.
12. Merge the pull request on GitHub.
    Use the merge button.
    Choose `Create a merge commit`.
    This option keeps individual commits.
    If your team wants one commit per feature, choose `Squash and merge`.
    Do not use `Rebase and merge` unless the team agrees.
13. After the merge, check that `main` passes all required checks.
14. Delete the remote feature branch after the merge.
15. Delete your local feature branch.
    Run `git checkout main`.
    Run `git pull`.
    Run `git branch -d feature/<short-name>`.

Hotfix workflow
1. Do not push directly to `main`. Use a pull request even for urgent fixes.
2. Create a hotfix branch from the latest `main`.
   Run `git checkout main`.
   Run `git pull`.
   Run `git checkout -b hotfix/<short-name>`.
3. Fix the issue on the hotfix branch.
4. Push the hotfix branch.
   Run `git push -u origin hotfix/<short-name>`.
5. Open a pull request from the hotfix branch to `main`.
6. Request an expedited review.
7. Merge the hotfix pull request after the checks pass.
8. After the merge, check that `main` passes all required checks.
9. Update all open feature branches with the hotfix.
   For each feature branch, merge `main` into the branch or rebase the branch onto `main`.
10. Delete the hotfix branch.

When to rebase or merge
- Rebase the feature branch only if you are the only developer on that branch.
- Rebase the feature branch before the merge to keep a linear history. This action is optional.
- Do not rebase a branch that other developers use.
- Merge `main` into a feature branch to integrate changes. This action does not rewrite the branch history.
- Merge a pull request to `main` with a merge commit.
- Use a hotfix branch and merge it to `main` before you update feature branches.

Spaced repetition schedules reviews at increasing intervals. Massed practice repeats material in one session. Massed practice has no increasing interval schedule. For long-term retention, spaced repetition is more effective than massed practice. Massed practice can produce fast short-term performance. That performance decays quickly without further spaced reviews.

Anki has a phase for new cards and a phase for review cards. New cards use default steps of 1 minute and 10 minutes. For review cards, the next interval depends on the answer button and the card's ease factor. The default ease factor is 2.5. A 1-day interval becomes about 2.5 days after a Good answer. Anki rounds this value to 2 or 3 days.

The review threshold is the answer quality that moves a card forward. Anki uses four answer buttons: Again, Hard, Good, Easy. Again marks the card as failed. It returns the card to the steps for new cards. Good applies the card's ease factor to the interval. Easy applies a larger multiplier.

Hard applies a smaller multiplier. You can use Hard to slow interval growth. Massed practice uses a threshold such as a number of consecutive correct answers. That threshold does not schedule future intervals.

When intervals grow too quickly, cards arrive after you forget them. Each failed card returns to a short interval. This adds extra reviews. A high number of lapses increases the daily workload. The daily workload can become a backlog. Too many new cards per day also create backlog.

You can reduce backlog risk with a low daily new-card limit. You can reserve the Easy button for cards that you know without effort. You can keep the default maximum interval or set a lower maximum interval. If a backlog forms, you can review the due cards first. You can suspend new cards until the backlog clears.

Likely causes

The cluster elects a new leader every 30 seconds. This interval matches a possible election timeout value. The exact behavior depends on the Raft implementation.

Three conditions can cause periodic elections. Network partitions isolate nodes and stop heartbeats. High disk I/O latency delays log writes on the leader. Election timeouts that are too short trigger elections during normal delays.

A network partition stops heartbeats between the leader and at least one follower. That follower starts an election after its timeout. A partition that lasts 30 seconds can cause this pattern.

High disk I/O latency on the leader can delay log replication and heartbeats. If the delay exceeds the election timeout, followers start elections.

A timeout value of 30 seconds can cause this pattern. If the leader does not send heartbeats for 30 seconds, followers start elections. Network partitions or disk delays can stop heartbeats for that duration.

Misconfigured election timeouts include values that are shorter than the heartbeat interval. A timeout that is too close to the heartbeat interval causes frequent elections. A typical configuration sets the heartbeat interval to less than half of the election timeout.

Diagnostic order

Before you start, collect access to the configuration files, the logs, and the metrics endpoint for each node.

Do not change configuration on a live cluster without a rollback plan. A wrong value can cause a loss of quorum.

1. Check the election timeout value and the heartbeat interval value on all three nodes.
2. Check that the values are identical on all nodes.
3. If the values differ, set all nodes to the same values.
4. Check the network latency and packet loss between each pair of nodes.
5. Check the disk I/O latency on each node.
6. Read the Raft log entries for repeated election messages and term increases.
7. If the election timeout is less than or equal to the heartbeat interval, increase the election timeout. Set the election timeout to at least three times the heartbeat interval.
8. If the network latency exceeds the heartbeat interval, reduce the network latency or increase the election timeout.
9. If the disk I/O latency exceeds the election timeout, reduce the disk latency or increase the election timeout.
10. After changes, monitor the cluster for 60 seconds. Check that no new election occurs.

# Materialized Views for a PostgreSQL Analytics Dashboard

Materialized views store query results as stored tables. A dashboard reads the stored data. A refresh updates the stored data. PostgreSQL provides `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` and `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY`. Materialized views are available in PostgreSQL 9.3 and later. Concurrent refresh is available in PostgreSQL 9.4 and later.

## Simple Refresh

The simple refresh method is `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW`.

- It replaces all rows.
- It takes an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock on the materialized view.
- That lock blocks concurrent reads and writes for the entire refresh.
- Index maintenance is automatic.
- It does not require a unique index.
- It is faster than concurrent refresh.
- It uses less temporary disk space.

## Concurrent Refresh

The concurrent refresh method is `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY`.

- It allows concurrent reads during the refresh.
- It requires a unique index.
- If the unique index is missing, the command fails.
- It creates a temporary table and applies row differences.
- It takes a short lock during the final data exchange.
- Only one concurrent refresh can run at a time for the same materialized view.
- Index maintenance is automatic.
- It is slower than simple refresh and uses more temporary disk space.
- Large materialized views require enough temporary disk space for this refresh.

## Materialized View Deletion and Recreation

A simple refresh does not drop and recreate the view. `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW` deletes the view and all its indexes. `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` creates a new view and runs the defining query. The view does not exist between the two statements. Queries in that window return errors. You must recreate indexes, grants, and dependent objects after the CREATE.

## Recommendation

Use `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` when the dashboard must not experience read downtime. The dashboard can continue to query the old data during the refresh. Use simple refresh when read downtime is acceptable, or when no unique index exists. Do not use `DROP` and `CREATE` for routine data refresh.

This procedure uses limits from the standard guidance for a CDL pre-trip inspection of a combination vehicle.
The typical governor cut-out is 120 to 125 psi.
Use the limits from the vehicle manual if they differ. The stricter limit takes precedence.

Safety first:
Park the combination on level ground.
Set the parking brakes.
Chock the tractor and trailer wheels.
Put the transmission in neutral.
Start the engine. Build air pressure to governor cut-out.
Stop the engine. Turn the ignition key to on. Do not start the engine.

A. Check the warning for low air pressure:
Watch the air pressure gauges.
Press and release the brake pedal several times.
Continue to press and release the brake pedal until the warning activates.
The warning must activate before the gauge reads below 60 psi.
If the warning activates at 59 psi or lower, stop the check. Do not drive.

B. Check spring brake application:
Continue to press and release the brake pedal.
The parking brake control and the trailer supply valve must pop out.
The typical pop-out range is 20 to 45 psi.
If either control pops out above 45 psi or below 20 psi, stop the check. Inspect the air system.
If the controls do not pop out before the gauge falls below 20 psi, stop the check. Do not drive.

C. Check air leakage rate:
Start the engine. Build pressure to governor cut-out again.
Stop the engine.
If the wheels are not chocked, do not release the parking brakes.
Release the parking brakes.
Set a timer for one minute. Read the gauge.
Wait one minute. Read the gauge.
The pressure drop with the brakes released must not exceed 3 psi for a combination vehicle.
Record a drop of 3 psi as a pass. Record a drop of 4 psi or more as a fail.
Set the parking brakes.
Set a timer for one minute. Read the gauge.
Press and hold the service brake pedal fully.
Wait for the gauge to stabilize. Do not count this initial drop.
Hold the pedal for one minute. Read the gauge.
The pressure drop with the service brakes applied must not exceed 4 psi after the initial drop.
Record a drop of 4 psi as a pass. Record a drop of 5 psi or more as a fail.

Edge cases:
If the warning activates at exactly 60 psi, treat it as a pass. Require no other fault and a vehicle manual that permits this threshold.
If a spring brake control pops out at exactly 20 psi or 45 psi, treat it as a pass. Require both controls to move fully.
If the movement is partial, inspect the air system before driving.
If the air leakage is exactly at the limit, pass only if no audible leak is heard. Also require that the gauge is stable after one minute.
If the gauge continues to fall, fail the check.

# Calibration and Measurement Uncertainty Evaluation for a 1000 µL Micropipette at the 100 µL Setting

## 1. Scope

This procedure describes the calibration and the measurement uncertainty evaluation for an adjustable micropipette with a nominal capacity of 1000 µL. The procedure applies to the lowest volume setting of 100 µL. The procedure meets the requirements of ISO/IEC 17025 for measurement traceability and uncertainty reporting. The uncertainty budget includes contributions from repeatability, balance linearity, dead volume, and operator technique.

## 2. References

- ISO 8655-2, Piston-operated volumetric apparatus – Part 2: Pipettes
- ISO/IEC 17025, General requirements for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories
- Manufacturer manual for the micropipette model

## 3. Equipment and Materials

- Analytical balance with a resolution of 0.01 mg and a valid calibration certificate
- Distilled or deionized water, degassed, at room temperature
- Calibrated thermometer with an uncertainty not greater than 0.1 °C
- Barometer or pressure sensor with an uncertainty not greater than 0.5 kPa
- Hygrometer with an uncertainty not greater than 5 % RH
- Disposable tips that fit the pipette model
- Container with a lid for weighing

## 4. Preliminary Verifications

Use these verifications before calibration. Do not proceed if any verification fails.

- Verify that the balance is level and calibrated.
- Verify that the balance is in a draft-free location.
- Verify that the air temperature is between 15 °C and 30 °C.
- Verify that the relative humidity is between 40 % and 80 %.
- Verify that the air pressure is between 86 kPa and 106 kPa.
- Record the environment values.
- Allow the water and the pipette to equilibrate for at least one hour.

## 5. Measurement Procedure

Follow these steps in order. Use one trained operator for all ten measurements.

1. Set the micropipette to 100 µL.
2. Attach a new tip.
3. Pre-wet the tip.
4. Aspirate and dispense water ten times.
5. After you pre-wet the tip, do not touch it.
6. Place the empty container on the balance pan.
7. Close the balance draft shield.
8. Tare the balance.
9. Aspirate water.
10. Immerse the tip 2 mm to 3 mm below the water surface.
11. Push the plunger to the first stop.
12. Release the plunger slowly.
13. Remove the tip from the water.
14. Touch the tip once to the inside wall of the source container.
15. Dispense the water into the container.
16. Touch the tip to the container wall above the water surface.
17. Withdraw the tip along the wall.
18. Close the draft shield.
19. Wait until the balance indication stabilizes.
20. Record the mass value.
21. Open the draft shield.
22. Remove the container from the balance.
23. Empty the container.
24. Repeat steps 6 through 23 for a total of ten measurements.

If a mass value deviates by more than 20 % from the expected mass, discard that value. Repeat the measurement.

Do not use a damaged tip. A damaged tip can leak and cause incorrect results.

## 6. Volume Calculation

### 6.1 Model

The operator calculates the delivered volume at 20 °C with this equation.

V = m × Z + δV_dead + δV_operator

Here:
- V is the delivered volume at 20 °C, in microliters.
- m is the observed mass, in milligrams.
- Z is the conversion factor from mass to volume for water at the measured temperature and air pressure.
- δV_dead is the correction for dead volume, in microliters.
- δV_operator is the correction for operator technique, in microliters.

### 6.2 Calculation Steps

- Obtain Z from ISO 8655-2 or from a certified reference table.
- Calculate the volume for each measurement with the equation.
- Calculate the mean volume and the experimental standard deviation from the ten results.

## 7. Uncertainty Evaluation

These sections describe the standard uncertainty components.

### 7.1 Repeatability

Repeatability is a Type A uncertainty component. The operator calculates the experimental standard deviation s of the ten volume results. The standard uncertainty of the mean volume is u_rep = s ÷ √10.

### 7.2 Balance Linearity

The balance calibration certificate gives the linearity value L in milligrams. The distribution is rectangular. The standard uncertainty from linearity is u_lin = (L ÷ √3) × Z.

### 7.3 Dead Volume

The dead volume is the liquid that remains in the tip after the operator dispenses the liquid. For a calibrated pipette with a correct tip, the mean dead volume correction δV_dead is zero. The laboratory estimates its standard uncertainty from the manufacturer's tip specification or from a separate gravimetric study. If no other estimate exists, the laboratory assumes a rectangular distribution with a half-width of 0.5 % of the nominal volume. The standard uncertainty is u_dead = 0.5 µL ÷ √3 = 0.29 µL for a nominal volume of 100 µL.

### 7.4 Operator Technique

The operator contribution includes repeatability between operators. The laboratory performs a reproducibility study with three trained operators. Each operator does ten measurements at 100 µL. The laboratory calculates the mean volume for each operator. The laboratory calculates the experimental standard deviation of the three operator means. The standard uncertainty from operator technique is u_operator = s_operators ÷ √3.

### 7.5 Combined Standard Uncertainty

The laboratory combines the components in quadrature with this equation.

u_c = √(u_rep² + u_lin² + u_dead² + u_operator²)

### 7.6 Expanded Uncertainty

The laboratory calculates the expanded uncertainty with a coverage factor k = 2.

U = 2 × u_c

The laboratory reports the calibration result as the mean volume ± U at a 95 % confidence level.

## 8. Decision Rule

The laboratory compares the result to the manufacturer's tolerance or to ISO 8655-2 limits. The micropipette passes calibration if the mean volume is within the tolerance and if U is less than one third of the tolerance. If U is greater than one third of the tolerance, the laboratory increases the number of measurements or reduces the uncertainty contributions.

## 9. Records

The calibration record includes these items.

- Pipette identification and operator name
- Environment temperature, pressure, and relative humidity
- Balance identification and calibration date
- Ten mass values and the calculated volumes
- Mean volume and experimental standard deviation
- Uncertainty budget and expanded uncertainty
- Pass or fail decision

## 10. Failure Handling

If the repeatability standard deviation is greater than expected, the laboratory finds the cause. The laboratory verifies the tip fit, the pipette seals, and the operator technique. The laboratory repeats the calibration after corrective action. If the environment is out of range, the laboratory stops the procedure. It stabilizes the room conditions before it continues.

The claim is incorrect. Platt scaling is not sufficient to guarantee calibration for a deep neural network classifier that uses label smoothing.

Label smoothing trains the model with soft target probabilities instead of one-hot labels. This process discourages very large logits. It reduces the confidence of predictions on the training data. Label smoothing often improves calibration for data from the same distribution. It does not guarantee correct probabilities for all inputs. Label smoothing can change the learned class probabilities away from the true posterior.

Platt scaling fits a logistic function to one scalar logit. For multiclass problems, an extension fits one logistic model per class. A logistic model per class still assumes a simple sigmoid relationship between the logit and the true probability. Label smoothing can change the logit distribution so that this relationship fails. Thus, Platt scaling is not a general solution for a label-smoothed deep network.

Temperature scaling multiplies all logits by one scalar parameter before the softmax. It preserves the rank order of predictions. It needs less calibration data than isotonic regression. For a label-smoothed model, the best temperature is often near 1.0. Temperature scaling cannot correct class-specific miscalibration. It applies the same scalar to all classes.

Isotonic regression fits a nonparametric monotonic step function to each class score. It can capture more complex calibration curves than a single scalar. It requires a larger calibration set. It can overfit small sets or produce piecewise constant probabilities. For a medical referral system, these probabilities affect patient risk decisions. Isotonic regression often achieves lower expected calibration error when the calibration set is large.

A medical system must not use Platt scaling as the only calibration method. The system must verify calibration on a held-out set. A proper scoring rule and the expected calibration error must measure calibration. If the calibration set is large, isotonic regression can give better per-class probabilities. If the calibration set is small, temperature scaling is safer. No calibration method guarantees calibrated probabilities under distribution shift. Medical referral systems also need decision thresholds that account for the cost of false negatives and false positives.

Quorum is the rule that a group must have more than half of its members before it can decide. For two etcd members, a majority is two. If one member is unreachable, neither member has a majority. etcd then stops serving requests. This state prevents leader election and key updates.

Fencing is a method to stop a node that is no longer the primary. In Patroni, the leader key in etcd gives one node the right to write. Patroni can use a watchdog to reset a node that does not release this right. If fencing fails, a former primary can continue to write. This failure causes split brain.

Patroni stores the leader identity in etcd. A node is primary only while it holds the leader key. Other nodes stay replicas. When the network between the two PostgreSQL nodes breaks, Patroni asks etcd which node is the leader. If etcd has quorum, it answers. If etcd does not have quorum, it cannot answer. This behavior depends on the Patroni version and the `failsafe_mode` setting.

Now examine the three causes.

1. An absent etcd tie-breaker
A two-member etcd cluster has quorum only when both members are online. A network split between the two members removes quorum. Patroni cannot read or update the leader key. If `failsafe_mode` is `true` on the replica, the replica can promote itself after a timeout. The old primary stays primary because it cannot contact etcd. This action creates split brain. This cause matches the symptom of two primary nodes after a brief interruption. It is the most likely cause.

2. A too-aggressive watchdog
A watchdog resets a node when Patroni is unresponsive. If the timeout is too short, the watchdog resets a healthy primary. Patroni then promotes the replica. This failover creates one primary at a time. The reset node reconnects later as a replica. A watchdog alone does not make two nodes primary at the same time after a brief interruption. This cause is less likely.

3. A firewall rule that blocks traffic between the nodes
If the firewall blocks only the PostgreSQL replication port (5432), the replica cannot copy data. The replica does not promote because the etcd leader key still belongs to the primary. If the firewall blocks etcd client traffic (2379) or etcd peer traffic (2380), the etcd cluster can lose quorum. This condition is the same as the absent tie-breaker. The firewall rule can trigger the partition, but the root cause is the lack of etcd quorum. A firewall rule alone is unlikely to cause two primary nodes.

To confirm the diagnosis, do these steps:

1. Run this command on each etcd member:
   etcdctl member list
   Confirm that the total number of etcd voting members is not two. If it is two, the cluster has no tie-breaker.

2. Inspect the Patroni configuration on both nodes. Look for `failsafe_mode`. If it is `true`, the replica can promote without the DCS. If the setting is absent, check the default for your Patroni version.

3. Check the firewall rules on both nodes. Run:
   sudo iptables -L -n
   Look for rules that block port 2379 or port 2380.

4. Read the Patroni logs on both nodes. Run:
   journalctl -u patroni --since `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS`
   Use the time of the incident. Look for messages about failsafe mode or promotion.

5. Restore quorum before you fix the roles. Add a third etcd member on a separate witness host. Do not run `patronictl switchover` until etcd has quorum again. The command can cause data loss if quorum is absent.

After you restore quorum, Patroni can elect one primary. The former primary can require `pg_rewind` or a fresh basebackup before it can rejoin as a replica. Follow the Patroni documentation for that step.

Local validation verifies a JWT access token from an OAuth2 provider. The token is a bearer token for a JSON API. The API enforces the Bearer scheme in the Authorization header. The API rejects a missing token, a malformed token, or a token with a wrong scheme.

Local validation includes these checks:

- The API verifies the signature with the provider's public key or shared secret. This check rejects tokens signed with an unexpected key or algorithm.
- The API checks that the `iss` claim equals the expected issuer.
- The API checks that the `aud` claim contains an identifier for this API or its client.
- The API rejects the token if the `exp` claim is in the past. It allows a small clock skew value only if the deployment can tolerate it.
- The API rejects the `alg` value `none`. It uses an algorithm allowlist and binds the key type to the algorithm.

Local validation is fast and does not require the provider at request time. It cannot see a revocation that occurs after token issuance. A revoked token remains accepted until the `exp` time plus any allowed clock skew. If access token lifetime is 60 seconds, local validation alone can accept a revoked token for up to 60 seconds plus any clock skew. For a requirement to reject revoked tokens within seconds of the revocation, local validation alone is not sufficient.

If the provider supports the token introspection endpoint, the API can call it for each request. The API must authenticate to the provider before the introspection call. The API sends the access token to the introspection endpoint. The response includes an `active` claim. The API must reject the token when `active` is false. This call can reject a revoked token within seconds, if the provider updates the revocation status quickly.

Introspection adds network latency to every request. It creates a dependency on the provider's availability and performance. If the provider is unavailable, the API must choose a failure policy. A policy that fails open accepts tokens when the introspection service is unavailable. A policy that fails closed rejects tokens when the introspection service is unavailable. A cache for introspection responses reduces provider load but delays revocation. For rejection within seconds, the cache lifetime must be shorter than the required delay.

Likely causes

KCl increases the ionic strength of the buffer. This increase changes the activity coefficients of the phosphate ions and hydrogen ions. The apparent pKa of the second phosphate group decreases. The glass electrode also sees a change in the liquid junction potential. This change occurs because the sample ionic strength differs from the calibration buffer ionic strength. These effects can lower the pH reading by several tenths of a pH unit. A change from 7.4 to 7.1 after 100 mM KCl is consistent with these effects.

For a phosphate buffer near pH 7.4, the pH decreases when the temperature increases. If the calibration buffer temperature and the sample temperature are different, the pH reading contains an error. The temperature compensation of a pH meter corrects only the electrode response. It does not correct the temperature dependence of the buffer pH.

Carbon dioxide from air dissolves in the buffer and forms carbonic acid. This acid can lower the pH slowly. The effect is small in a 50 mM phosphate buffer unless the solution is open and stirred for hours. The immediate pH decrease after KCl addition is not consistent with CO2 absorption alone.

Adjustment procedure

Use the procedure below to keep the pH at 7.4 when you add KCl.

1. Dissolve the required phosphate salts in water.
2. Add KCl to a final concentration of 100 mM.
3. Stir the solution until the salts dissolve.
4. Set the pH meter temperature compensation to the assay temperature.
5. Calibrate the pH meter with standard buffers at the assay temperature.
6. Measure the pH.
7. If the pH is less than 7.40, add a small volume of 1 M sodium hydroxide.
8. Stir the solution.
9. Measure the pH again.
10. Repeat steps 7 through 9 until the pH reaches 7.40.
11. If the pH becomes greater than 7.40, add a small volume of 1 M hydrochloric acid.
12. Stir the solution.
13. Measure the pH again.
14. Bring the solution to the final volume with water.
15. Verify the final pH.
16. If the pH is outside 7.40, adjust the pH again.
17. Keep the solution covered when you do not measure the pH.

Correlation is a statistical relation between two variables. A change in one variable tends to occur with a change in the other variable. Causation is a stronger claim. A change in one variable produces a change in the other variable.

A strong correlation does not prove causation. Three common alternative explanations can create a correlation without a causal link:

- A third variable causes both correlated variables. For example, hot weather increases ice cream sales and the number of drownings. Ice cream does not cause drownings.
- The causal direction is reversed. A correlation between variable A and variable B can exist because B causes A, not because A causes B.
- The correlation is a coincidence or a result of selection bias.

To tell them apart in data, you must use methods that address these alternatives. Observational data alone cannot prove causation without strong assumptions. You can use these methods:

- You can check that the cause precedes the effect in time.
- You can control for confounders with regression or matched samples.
- You can look for a dose-response relation.
- You can use random assignment in an experiment when possible.

A strong correlation alone does not justify a causal claim. The alternatives above can explain the same data. For a causal claim, you must eliminate these alternatives with evidence.

Example: Many studies found a correlation between smoking and lung cancer. This correlation is strong. Scientists used many types of evidence, including laboratory studies and biological mechanisms, to rule out confounders and reverse causation. Therefore, the causal claim that smoking causes lung cancer is accepted. In contrast, the correlation between ice cream sales and drownings is strong in summer months. The third variable, hot weather, explains this correlation. Ice cream does not cause drownings.

Correlation describes a pattern in data. Causation requires a specific mechanism and evidence from controlled studies. You must not infer causation from correlation alone.

The claim is misleading. Traffic flow theory does not support a universal rule that extra lanes reduce congestion. Extra lanes can increase throughput for a short time. They do not guarantee less delay after travel patterns change.

A highway section has a maximum outflow at each bottleneck. The fundamental diagram of traffic flow shows that a bottleneck sets the maximum sustainable flow. If a bottleneck is downstream, extra lanes upstream do not increase that outflow. The queue can move to a new location or return when demand grows. This behavior is common when the downstream road, ramp, or intersection limits flow.

Induced demand refers to extra trips that appear after capacity increases. People move, change route, or drive more because the new road seems faster. This effect often fills the added capacity over time. As a result, delay can return to the level that existed before the capacity increase.

Extra lanes can reduce congestion only under narrow conditions. The extra lanes must remove the bottleneck that limits flow. The downstream system must have enough capacity to accept the higher flow. Travel demand must not grow enough to erase the gain. These conditions seldom hold in large urban networks.

Therefore, extra lanes are not a reliable general method to reduce congestion. A full corridor analysis must include downstream capacity and the expected demand response.

The Industrial Revolution was the change from hand production to machine production. It began in Britain in the late 18th century. Then it spread to other parts of Europe, North America, and Japan.

Important terms include the following:
- Industrialization means the growth of factory production.
- Factory system means production in a central workplace with machines and wage labor.
- Mechanization means the use of machines to replace hand work.
- Urbanization means the growth of cities.

Britain had several conditions that supported early industrialization.
- Large coal and iron deposits were close to each other.
- Rivers and canals supplied cheap transport.
- Capital came from Atlantic trade and colonial markets.
- Farm improvements released workers for industry.
No single condition caused the change.

Mechanization began in the textile industry. James Hargreaves invented the spinning jenny about 1764. Richard Arkwright patented the water frame in 1769. Samuel Crompton combined these designs in the spinning mule in 1779. Edmund Cartwright patented the power loom in 1785. James Watt improved the steam engine in the 1760s and 1770s.

Iron makers used coke instead of charcoal after Abraham Darby's work in 1709. Henry Cort patented a process in 1784, and that process made wrought iron in large amounts. The Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in 1825. The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in 1830. Factories expanded because the steam engine no longer depended on water power. Steam power allowed factories to move away from rivers.

The factory system changed work. Workers sold their labor for wages. They worked fixed shifts under supervision. Machines set the pace of work. The division of labor broke production into small tasks. Child labor was common in textile mills and mines.

Cities grew quickly. Manchester became a center of cotton production. Housing and sanitation did not keep pace with that growth. Pollution from coal smoke darkened the air. Disease spread in crowded districts.

Factory work separated paid work from the home. For many families in factory districts, all members worked for wages. Women and children often worked in mills and mines. The household lost some of its role in production. For many of these families, the home became a place for domestic tasks more than for paid production. Later laws limited child labor and set limits on the hours of work.

Historians debate the exact weight of each condition. Historians use the term for a long process with uneven timing. The Industrial Revolution did not change all trades or regions at the same rate. It spread from Britain over the 19th century.

Infrastructure as code is a method to manage cloud resources with text files. These files describe the desired state of cloud resources. A tool applies the files to create or change resources. This method replaces manual changes in a web console.

You store the files in a version control system. You review and record each change. You can use the same file for many resources. That reduces differences between environments. This practice helps prevent configuration mistakes, but it does not remove all risk. A wrong value in the file still causes a wrong configuration.

If a resource fails, you can read the file to see the intended state. You can compare the intended state with the actual state. Some tools can detect drift automatically. Drift is a difference between the file and the live resource. You can apply the file again to restore the intended state. This restore can delete or replace data, and the result depends on the resource type and the tool.

If a change causes a failure, you can use version control to return to an earlier file. This return is not a formal guarantee. The external resource must accept the earlier configuration.

The sender uses HMAC-SHA256 to sign a string that contains a timestamp, a nonce, and the payload.
The sender must choose a unique nonce for each request.
The receiver checks the signature and then checks that the timestamp is within a set window.
If the timestamp fails, the receiver rejects the request and does not record the nonce.
If the timestamp passes, the receiver records the nonce and rejects a repeated nonce within that window.

For Design B, the sender signs only the payload with the shared secret.
In this comparison, Design B does not add a timestamp or a nonce.
The receiver checks the signature.
It does not check time or nonce.

For replay protection, Design A rejects a repeated request if the nonce is already in the store.
The store must keep each nonce for at least as long as the timestamp window.
A replay attempt after the window fails because the timestamp is too old.
Design B has no time check and no nonce check.
An attacker can store a valid signed request and send it again at any later time.
The receiver will accept it unless the payload contains a unique identifier and the receiver tracks that identifier.

For clock skew, Design A can reject a valid request when the sender clock and the receiver clock differ by more than the allowed window.
A larger window accepts more clock skew, but the receiver must keep each nonce for the duration of that larger window.
The nonce check stops a replay within the window.
Design B has no timestamp check.
Clock skew does not cause a false rejection for this design.

A legitimate webhook can arrive after the replay window.
Design A rejects it.
The signature is valid and the nonce is new, but the timestamp is too old.
The sender must retry with a new timestamp, a new nonce, and a new signature.
The receiver can then check the retry.
If the receiver already processed the same event through another path, the application must handle duplicate data.

Design B accepts a delayed legitimate webhook because no time check exists.
This property permits delayed delivery.
But that same property means that an attacker can replay the request at any time unless another control prevents it.

Do these checks in this order:
1. Check the firewall rule order.
2. Check that the allow rule for this service is before any deny rule.
3. Check the protocol and destination port in the allow rule.
4. Check that the firewall permits return traffic for this connection.
5. Check that the stateful inspection feature is enabled.
6. Check that the firewall state table contains the TCP connection.
7. Check the service status on the destination host.
8. Check that the service listens on the correct IP address and port.
9. Check the host firewall rules for the service port.
10. Check that the service access control list permits the source address.
11. Check the network address translation rules.
12. Check that the NAT rule forwards the port to the correct host.
13. Check the firewall logs for denied packets.

The following structured techniques clarify vague requirements and contradictions:

- Requirements workshop. A facilitator guides stakeholders to define terms and resolve conflicts.
- Structured interview. Ask open questions first, then ask about data, timing, error paths, and constraints.
- Use case or user story. Each story contains acceptance criteria in Given-When-Then format.
- Decision table. List condition combinations and outcomes for complex business rules.
- Dependency map. Trace each data element, interface, and external system to its source and consumer.

For each requirement, ask what must be true before the feature functions. This question reveals hidden dependencies such as input data availability, external system readiness, and access rights. Also ask what can fail when the feature runs in production. Include negative acceptance criteria for failure paths such as invalid input, timeout, and permission denial. Acceptance criteria must have measurable thresholds. For example, state "The system returns result R within 2 seconds for 1,000 rows."

After the first draft, create a requirements baseline. The baseline is a versioned set that the sponsors approve. All later changes must enter a change control process. The change request must describe the impact on schedule, cost, and other requirements. Use a traceability matrix to link each requirement to its source, design element, and test case. When a requirement changes, the matrix shows all affected items.

Record each decision in a decision log with a reason. This log captures why a requirement changed, so that the team can trace the change later.

Architecture decisions that involve conflicting non-functional requirements need a written trade-off analysis.
First, the analysis defines each requirement as a measurable property.
For example, low latency can mean a maximum 99th percentile response time.
Strong consistency can mean that every read returns the value of the latest acknowledged write.
These definitions remove ambiguity.

The analysis then identifies the conflict.
The CAP theorem states that during a network partition, a distributed system cannot provide both consistency and availability.
This theorem does not cover latency directly.
Strong consistency often increases latency because a write must wait for acknowledgment from multiple replicas.
A design can choose lower latency with weaker consistency or stronger consistency with higher latency.

For each candidate option, the analysis quantifies latency, consistency level, availability, and operation cost.
Measurements can come from prototypes or published benchmarks.
The analysis states the load, the data size, and the failure model.
A comparison table can show these values for each option.
The analysis weighs each requirement according to system priorities.
A multi-criteria decision method can make the ranking explicit.

A decision record stores the result of the trade-off analysis.
A common template includes these sections: Title, Status, Context, Options, Decision, Rationale, and Consequences.
The Context section lists the conflicting requirements and the measured constraints.
The Options section includes the quantified impact of each rejected option.
The Decision section states the chosen architecture pattern and its configuration.
The Rationale and Consequences sections explain the choice, the limitations, the risks, and the rollback plan.

The team reviews the decision record when a requirement or a measurement changes.
The team can then update the record or replace it with a new version.

No, that assumption is not always true. A covering index includes every column that the query references in any clause. In many database engines, a covering index lets the engine return all values and does not read the base table. Some engines still perform physical reads of the base table in specific situations.

PostgreSQL can perform an index-only scan. It still reads heap pages when the visibility map does not show that all tuples are visible to the current transaction. This occurs after updates or deletes until the cleanup process refreshes the map. The query result remains correct, but the scan touches the base table.

A covering index can hurt performance. A wide index uses more storage and memory. Inserts, updates, and deletes become slower because the database must maintain more index columns. A scan of a large range can read more pages than a scan of a smaller key-only index.

A query that filters on an expression of a column can force a full scan of the index. The index still contains the column value, so the scan does not read the base table. But a full scan can be much slower than a seek that uses an expression index. Type conversion or collation mismatch can cause a similar full scan.

The exact behavior depends on the database product, version, and configuration. The examples above are common but not universal.

Complete these steps to publish a payload with acquire and release.

1. Define a shared non-atomic payload object that both threads can access.
2. Define a shared std::atomic<bool> flag with initial value false.
3. Use the same flag for the release store and the acquire load.
4. Use this pattern for one writer thread only.
5. Use a mutex if more than one thread writes the payload.
6. In the writer thread, write all payload fields before you set the flag.
7. After the payload write, call flag.store(true, std::memory_order_release).
8. In the reader thread, call flag.load(std::memory_order_acquire) in a loop until it returns true.
9. After the acquire load returns true, read the payload fields.
10. Do not write the payload after the release store.
11. Do not read the payload before the acquire load returns true.
12. Keep the payload object alive until the reader thread completes all reads.

Check these conditions before you run the program:
- Check that the release store happens after all payload writes.
- Check that the acquire load reads the value from that release store.
- Check that the payload writes happen before the payload reads per the C++ memory model.

Investigate these underlying causes first:
- Check if the budget uses optimistic assumptions for price, volume, or productivity.
- Check if salaries, benefits, energy, or supplier prices increase faster than the forecast assumes.
- Check if the department adds tasks or services without a matching budget increase.
- Check if equipment failures, legal costs, or emergencies consume budget that was not reserved for them.
- Check if costs from other periods or categories appear in the wrong quarter.
- Check if purchase approvals and budget checks do not stop new commitments.
Then take these typical immediate corrective actions:
- Freeze discretionary expenditures and rebalance the budget.
- Reforecast with conservative assumptions based on actual cost trends from the last three quarters.
- Require budget owner approval for all new non-payroll expenditure.
- Reallocate funds from underspent categories to categories with persistent overruns.
- Hold weekly variance reviews and act on large variances immediately.
- Audit the forecast process to remove optimism bias and include known cost drivers.
